For 1 → 4 → 9 and 2 → 3 → 10, the result is 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 9 → 10. It takes O(n + m) time and only relinks existing nodes, which is the heart of merge sort on linked lists.

Deleting the whole list: In C, when you are finished with a list you must free every node. Walk through it, but save the next pointer before freeing the current node: while (head != NULL) { t = head; head = head->next; free(t); }. If you free first and then read t->next, you are reading freed memory, the dangling pointer bug from the last lesson.

Recap: A singly linked list is a chain of nodes, each with data and a next pointer, starting at head and ending at NULL. Traversal and search are O(n). Inserting or deleting at the front is O(1); at the end it is O(n), or O(1) for insertion with a tail pointer. Inserting after a known node is O(1). Reversal uses three pointers in O(n). Linked lists trade O(1) index access for cheap, copy-free growth and relinking. Next, we add backward pointers and circular links.
key_points: A singly linked list is a chain of nodes; each node has data and a next pointer; the last next is NULL.
head points to the first node; never move head while traversing.
Traversal and search are O(n); insert or delete at the front is O(1).
Insert after a known node in O(1): n->next = p->next; then p->next = n.
Deleting a node needs its previous node; deleting the last node is O(n) even with a tail pointer.
Reverse with three pointers (prev, cur, next) in O(n) time and O(1) space.
Linked lists trade O(1) index access for cheap insertion and no resizing.
lessons.tip: Before writing any linked list code, draw the boxes and arrows, then number each pointer change in the order you will do it. If an arrow you still need disappears, swap the order.
lessons.task: Take 5 small paper slips and write a number on each. Lay them out on a table and use strings or drawn arrows as next pointers. Act out insert-at-front, delete-by-value and reverse, moving only the arrows, never the slips.

quiz.q: What does the next pointer of the last node in a singly linked list hold?
quiz.explain: NULL marks the end of the list.

quiz.q: What is the time to insert at the front of a singly linked list?
quiz.explain: Create the node, point it at head, and move head: a constant number of steps.

quiz.q: To insert node n after node p, which order is correct?
quiz.explain: Link n to the rest first; otherwise the rest of the list is lost.

quiz.q: Why is binary search not efficient on a linked list?
options: There is no O(1) way to reach the middle node
quiz.explain: Reaching the middle requires walking node by node.

quiz.q: Reversing a singly linked list with three pointers takes:
options: O(n) time and O(1) extra space
quiz.explain: Each node's pointer is flipped once using only prev, cur and next.

lessons.title: Doubly and Circular Linked Lists
lessons.content:
Picture a line of children holding hands in a school assembly. In a singly linked list, each child only holds the hand of the child in front, so a message can only travel forwards. Now let each child hold both neighbours' hands. A message can travel forwards or backwards, and if one child steps out, the two neighbours simply grab each other. Finally, imagine the last child also holds hands with the first, closing the line into a circle for a game of passing the parcel. Those three pictures are the singly, doubly and circular linked lists.

Why we need more than singly linked lists: In the last lesson we hit two walls. First, you cannot move backwards, so deleting a node requires finding the node before it by walking from the head. Second, deleting the last node is O(n) even with a tail pointer. A doubly linked list fixes both by giving every node a pointer to its previous node as well. A circular list fixes a different problem: when you need to loop around a collection again and again.

Doubly linked list, what it is: Each node has three parts: a prev pointer, the data, and a next pointer. In C: struct DNode { struct DNode *prev; int data; struct DNode *next; };. The first node's prev is NULL and the last node's next is NULL. We usually keep both a head and a tail pointer. For 10 ⇄ 20 ⇄ 30: 10's prev is NULL, 10's next is 20, 20's prev is 10, 20's next is 30, 30's prev is 20, and 30's next is NULL.

Traversal both ways: Forward traversal is the same as before: p = head; while (p) { print(p->data); p = p->next; }. Backward traversal starts at the tail: p = tail; while (p) { print(p->data); p = p->prev; }, printing 30, 20, 10. Both are O(n). Being able to walk backwards is exactly what a music player's previous button, or a browser's back and forward history, needs.

Insert at the front of a doubly linked list: Create n with data 5. Set n->prev = NULL and n->next = head. If the list is not empty, set head->prev = n; otherwise set tail = n. Finally head = n. Four small pointer updates instead of two, but still O(1). The key habit is that every link now has two directions, so whenever you create a link you must set both halves.

Insert after a node p: To insert n after p: n->prev = p; n->next = p->next; if (p->next != NULL) p->next->prev = n; else tail = n; p->next = n;. For 10 ⇄ 20 ⇄ 30, inserting 25 after 20 gives 10 ⇄ 20 ⇄ 25 ⇄ 30. Notice we change four pointers: n's two pointers, 30's prev and 20's next. As always, set the new node's pointers first, then redirect the old nodes, so nothing gets lost.

Delete a given node p in O(1): This is the big win. If you have a pointer p to the node to delete, you no longer need to search for the previous node, because p->prev is right there. if (p->prev) p->prev->next = p->next; else head = p->next; if (p->next) p->next->prev = p->prev; else tail = p->prev; free(p);. Deleting the last node is now O(1) too: p = tail. The two neighbours simply hold hands with each other, like the children in the assembly.

Cost of doubly linked lists: Each node stores an extra pointer, so the memory per node grows (on a 64-bit machine, 8 more bytes per node). Every insertion and deletion must update more pointers, so the code is longer and has more chances for bugs. In return, you get backward traversal and O(1) deletion of a known node. Many real libraries, for example C++'s std::list and Java's LinkedList, are doubly linked.

Circular singly linked list: In a circular list, the last node's next pointer points back to the first node instead of NULL. There is no natural end, so traversal must stop when it returns to the starting node: if (head) { p = head; do { print(p->data); p = p->next; } while (p != head); }. Using a do-while matters: with a plain while (p != head) the loop would stop immediately.

Keeping a pointer to the last node: A clever trick for circular lists is to keep a pointer to the last node, often called last, instead of head. Then the first node is simply last->next. Inserting at the front becomes: n->next = last->next; last->next = n;. Inserting at the end is the same plus last = n;. Both are O(1) with a single pointer, which is why circular lists are often managed through last.

Circular doubly linked list: Combine both ideas: each node has prev and next, the last node's next points to the first, and the first node's prev points to the last. Now from any node you can move forwards or backwards forever, and both ends are reachable in O(1). This is a common choice for implementing a deque, and many textbooks use a circular doubly linked list with a header node, where the empty list is just a header pointing to itself in both directions.

Where circular lists shine: Anything that goes round in turns. An operating system's round-robin scheduler gives each running program a small time slice, then moves to the next, and after the last program it comes back to the first. A circular list models that perfectly. Multiplayer board games, like ludo with four players, also cycle through turns. The classic Josephus problem, where people in a circle are eliminated every k-th turn, is solved neatly by deleting nodes from a circular list.

A worked Josephus example: Five people numbered 1 to 5 stand in a circle, and every second person is removed, starting the count at person 1. Count 1, 2: remove 2. From 3, count 3, 4: remove 4. From 5, count 5, 1: remove 1. From 3, count 3, 5: remove 5. Person 3 is the survivor. With a circular linked list, each removal is just 'skip one, unlink the next', which is easy to code and to trace by hand.

Polynomial representation: A linked list is a natural way to store a polynomial like 5x³ + 4x² + 2. Each non-zero term becomes a node with a coefficient, an exponent and a next pointer: (5, 3) → (4, 2) → (2, 0). Terms are kept in decreasing order of exponent. Zero terms are not stored, so a sparse polynomial like x^1000 + 1 needs only two nodes instead of an array of 1,001 slots.

Polynomial addition: To add P = 5x³ + 4x² + 2 and Q = 3x³ + 6x + 1, walk through both lists at once, like merging. Compare the exponents at the front. If they are equal (3 and 3), add the coefficients (5 + 3 = 8) and output (8, 3), moving both. If P's exponent is larger, copy P's term and move P; if Q's is larger, copy Q's term and move Q. Continue: (4, 2) from P, (6, 1) from Q, then (2, 0) and (1, 0) add to (3, 0). Result: 8x³ + 4x² + 6x + 3. It takes O(m + n) for m and n terms. If coefficients add to zero, skip that term.

Polynomial multiplication, briefly: Multiply every term of P by every term of Q (multiply coefficients, add exponents), then combine terms with equal exponents. With m and n terms that is m × n products. The combining step is easier if you insert each product into a result list kept sorted by exponent. Exams more often ask addition, but knowing the idea of multiplication helps.

Choosing between list types: Use a singly linked list when you only move forwards and memory is tight, for example a simple stack. Use a doubly linked list when you need to delete arbitrary known nodes quickly or move both ways, for example an LRU cache or an editor's undo/redo history. Use a circular list when the data is naturally cyclic, such as turns or round-robin scheduling.

Real life example 1, the browser's back and forward buttons: When you browse from Prothom Alo to a sports page to a cricket score page, the history can be a doubly linked list. Back moves to prev, forward moves to next. If you go back two pages and then open a new link, everything after the current node is cut off and the new page is attached as the next node. All of these moves are O(1) pointer changes.

Real life example 2, the LRU cache in apps like Facebook: An app keeps recently viewed images in memory, but space is limited. When it is full, it throws out the least recently used image. A common design uses a doubly linked list ordered from most recent to least recent, plus a hash table that maps an image ID straight to its node. Viewing an image moves its node to the front in O(1) (delete it with prev and next, insert at head). Evicting removes the tail in O(1). This combination is a famous interview design question.

Real life example 3, carrom or ludo turns: In a four-player ludo game at a family gathering, turns pass 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 1 → 2 and so on. If one player leaves, their node is removed from the circle and the game keeps flowing. A circular list models this exactly, without any 'if last player, go back to first' special code.

Common mistakes: In doubly linked lists, updating next but forgetting prev (or the other way round), which leaves the list broken in one direction. Forgetting to update head or tail when inserting or deleting at an end. In circular lists, using while (p != NULL), which loops forever because there is no NULL, or using while (p != head) without do-while, which never runs. In polynomial addition, forgetting to copy the leftover terms of the longer list.

What exams ask: Define doubly and circular linked lists with diagrams. Write algorithms for insertion and deletion in a doubly linked list. Explain why deleting a known node is O(1) in a doubly but O(n) in a singly linked list. Traverse a circular list. Represent a polynomial using a linked list and add two polynomials step by step. Compare singly, doubly and circular lists in a table.

Recap: A doubly linked list gives each node prev and next pointers, enabling backward traversal and O(1) deletion of a known node, at the cost of extra memory and more pointer updates. A circular list links the last node back to the first, perfect for round-robin problems, and is often handled through a pointer to the last node. Linked lists also represent polynomials neatly, and adding two polynomials is a merge-like walk in O(m + n).
key_points: A doubly linked list node has prev, data and next pointers.
Doubly linked lists allow backward traversal and O(1) deletion of a known node.
Every insertion in a doubly linked list must set links in both directions.
In a circular list, the last node points back to the first; traverse with a do-while until you return.
Keeping a pointer to the last node gives O(1) insert at both front and end of a circular list.
Circular lists fit round-robin scheduling, turn-based games and the Josephus problem.
Polynomials are stored as (coefficient, exponent) nodes; addition is a merge in O(m + n).
lessons.tip: For doubly linked lists, count the arrows: inserting a node in the middle changes exactly four pointers, deleting changes exactly two. If your code changes a different number, look again.
lessons.task: Write the polynomials 7x⁴ + 3x² + 5 and 2x⁴ + 4x³ − 3x² + 1 as chains of (coefficient, exponent) boxes on paper. Add them using two fingers walking down both chains, and write the result chain.

quiz.q: What extra pointer does a doubly linked list node have compared to a singly linked node?
options: A pointer to the previous node
quiz.explain: Each node also points to its previous node.

quiz.q: In a doubly linked list, deleting a node p that you already have a pointer to takes:
quiz.explain: p->prev and p->next are directly available, so only neighbours' pointers change.

quiz.q: Why should traversal of a circular list use a do-while loop when stopping at head?
options: Because a plain while (p != head) would stop before visiting anything
Because circular lists cannot be traversed
quiz.explain: p starts equal to head, so the condition must be checked after the first visit.

quiz.q: Adding 5x³ + 4x² + 2 and 3x³ + 6x + 1 gives:
quiz.explain: Add coefficients of equal exponents; copy the others.

quiz.q: Which application suits a circular linked list best?
quiz.explain: Round robin cycles through processes and returns to the first after the last.

lessons.title: Stacks: Last In, First Out
lessons.content:
Walk into any wedding community centre in Dhaka and look at the stack of clean plates near the buffet. The staff put washed plates on top, and guests take plates from the top. Nobody pulls a plate from the bottom; the whole pile would crash. The plate that went on last is the first one taken. This simple rule, last in, first out, is the whole idea of a stack, one of the most useful structures in computer science.

What it is: A stack is a linear data structure where insertion and deletion happen only at one end, called the top. The rule is LIFO: Last In, First Out. Adding an item is called push, removing the top item is called pop, and looking at the top item without removing it is called peek (or top). We also usually have isEmpty, which checks whether the stack has no items, and sometimes isFull for a fixed-size stack, plus size.

The stack ADT: As we learned in lesson one, an ADT describes behaviour, not implementation. The Stack ADT says: push(x) puts x on top; pop() removes and returns the top item; peek() returns the top item without removing it; isEmpty() returns true if there are no items. All four should be O(1). It says nothing about arrays or pointers; we will build it both ways.

A trace: Start with an empty stack. push(10): stack is [10] with 10 on top. push(20): [10, 20], top is 20. push(30): [10, 20, 30], top is 30. pop() returns 30, leaving [10, 20]. peek() returns 20 and leaves the stack unchanged. push(40): [10, 20, 40]. pop() returns 40. pop() returns 20. pop() returns 10. Now the stack is empty, and another pop() would be an error. Practise writing traces like this; they are in nearly every exam.

Array implementation: Use an array stack[MAX] and an integer top that holds the index of the top item. Start with top = −1, meaning empty. push(x): if top == MAX − 1, report overflow; else top = top + 1; stack[top] = x. pop(): if top == −1, report underflow; else x = stack[top]; top = top − 1; return x. peek(): return stack[top] if not empty. isEmpty(): return top == −1. Every operation is O(1).

Overflow and underflow: Stack overflow happens when you try to push onto a full fixed-size stack. Stack underflow happens when you try to pop from an empty stack. Both must be checked in code; exam algorithms that skip these checks lose marks. With a dynamic array (like a Python list or C++ vector) overflow effectively disappears, because the array grows, and push becomes O(1) amortized.

Linked list implementation: Use a singly linked list where the head is the top. push(x): create node n; n->next = top; top = n. pop(): if top == NULL, underflow; else t = top; x = t->data; top = top->next; free(t); return x. Both are O(1), because we only work at the front of the list, which is exactly where singly linked lists are fast. There is no overflow unless the whole memory runs out, but each item costs an extra pointer.

Array versus linked implementation: The array version is simpler, faster in practice thanks to cache friendliness, and uses less memory per item, but has a fixed capacity unless you use a dynamic array. The linked version grows freely one node at a time but costs a pointer per item and a memory allocation per push. For most programs, a dynamic array based stack is the usual choice.

Two stacks in one array: A classic trick stores two stacks in a single array of size n. Stack 1 grows from the left (top1 starts at −1 and increases) and stack 2 grows from the right (top2 starts at n and decreases). Overflow happens only when top1 + 1 == top2, meaning the two tops meet. This uses the space efficiently: either stack can use any free space, instead of each being stuck with half the array.

The call stack: Every time your program calls a function, the computer pushes a block of information, called a stack frame or activation record, onto the call stack. It holds the function's parameters, local variables and the return address (where to continue afterwards). When the function returns, its frame is popped. If main calls f and f calls g, the frames are main, f, g from bottom to top, and g finishes first. This is why we will study recursion with stacks in mind.

Stack overflow in real programs: The call stack has limited size. If a function calls itself forever, for example a recursion with no base case, frames keep piling up until the stack runs out of room, and the program crashes with a stack overflow error. The famous programming Q&A website Stack Overflow is named after this error.

Undo and redo: Text editors, Photoshop and even Microsoft Word keep your actions on an undo stack. Typing a word pushes an action. Pressing Ctrl+Z pops the most recent action and reverses it. Many editors also keep a redo stack: an undone action is pushed onto the redo stack, so Ctrl+Y can pop it back. If you make a new edit after undoing, the redo stack is cleared, because the old future no longer makes sense.

Reversing with a stack: Push every item of a sequence onto a stack, then pop them all: they come out in reverse order. To reverse "DHAKA": push D, H, A, K, A, then pop A, K, A, H, D, giving "AKAHD". Reversing a word, reversing a linked list without changing pointers, and checking palindromes can all be done this way in O(n).

Other famous uses: Checking balanced brackets in code, converting infix expressions like (a + b) × c to postfix, and evaluating postfix expressions; these get their own lesson next. Backtracking problems, such as solving a maze by trying a path and backing up when stuck, use a stack to remember the path. Depth-first search on graphs uses a stack, which we will see in the graph traversal lesson.

A maze, step by step: Imagine walking through a maze drawn on a grid. At each cell, you push your position and try an unvisited neighbour. If you reach a dead end, you pop to go back to the previous cell and try another direction. The stack always holds the path from the start to where you are now. When you reach the exit, the stack contents are the path. If the stack becomes empty, there is no way out.

Real life example 1, the browser back button: When you open bdnews24, then click to a sports article, then to a photo gallery, the browser pushes each page onto a back stack. Pressing back pops the gallery and shows the article. Pressing back again pops the article and shows the homepage. Because the most recent page must come first, a stack is the perfect fit. Combined with a forward stack, it gives the full back and forward feature.

Real life example 2, a tiffin carrier: The classic stacked steel tiffin box that office workers carry in Dhaka has bowls on top of each other: rice at the bottom, then dal, then curry on top. To get to the rice, you must first remove the curry bowl, then the dal bowl. The last bowl put on is the first one you take off. That is a stack in your hands at lunchtime.

Real life example 3, a pile of exam scripts: A teacher collects answer scripts as students submit them, placing each on top of the pile. When checking, she takes from the top, so the last student to submit gets checked first. If she wants the first submitted script, she has to dig through the whole pile, which is exactly why stacks do not offer access to the bottom.

Common mistakes: Confusing stack (LIFO) with queue (FIFO). Starting top at 0 instead of −1 and then being off by one in the full and empty checks. Forgetting overflow and underflow checks. In the linked version, forgetting to free the popped node in C. Calling peek or pop on an empty stack. Thinking you can access the middle element of a stack in O(1); the ADT does not allow it, even if the array underneath could.

What exams ask: Define a stack and its operations. Write push and pop algorithms for array and linked list implementations, with overflow and underflow checks. Trace a sequence of pushes and pops and give the final stack and the popped values. Explain the call stack and stack overflow. Implement two stacks in one array. List applications of stacks.

A typical trace question: 'Show the stack after: push(5), push(9), pop(), push(3), push(7), pop(), push(1).' Work it out: [5], [5, 9], pop returns 9 → [5], [5, 3], [5, 3, 7], pop returns 7 → [5, 3], [5, 3, 1]. Final stack from bottom to top: 5, 3, 1, and the popped values in order: 9, 7.

A sneaky question: If 1, 2, 3 are pushed in that order, but pops can happen at any time in between, which output orders are possible? 1 2 3 (push, pop each time), 3 2 1 (push all, pop all), 2 1 3, 1 3 2 and 2 3 1 are possible. But 3 1 2 is impossible: to output 3 first, 1 and 2 must already be in the stack with 2 on top, so 2 must come out before 1. Exams love this kind of question.

Stacks in everyday code: You rarely have to build a stack from scratch at work. In Python you use a list with append and pop. In Java you can use ArrayDeque with push and pop (the older Stack class still exists, but ArrayDeque is the usual recommendation). In C++ there is std::stack, which wraps a vector or deque underneath. Knowing how they work inside still matters, because it tells you that these operations are O(1), and it helps you write a stack yourself in a language or exam where none is provided.

A min-stack puzzle: Interviewers sometimes ask for a stack that can also return the minimum item in O(1). The trick is to keep a second stack of minimums. When you push x, also push min(x, current minimum) onto the min stack. When you pop, pop both. The top of the min stack is always the minimum of everything currently stored. Push 5, 3, 7: the min stack holds 5, 3, 3, so getMin returns 3; after popping 7 and 3, it returns 5.

Recap: A stack allows insertion and deletion only at the top, following LIFO. Push, pop, peek and isEmpty all run in O(1). With an array, track top starting at −1 and check overflow and underflow; with a linked list, use the head as the top. Stacks power function calls, undo, back buttons, reversal, backtracking and depth-first search. Next, we will use stacks to read and evaluate arithmetic expressions.
key_points: A stack is LIFO: the last item pushed is the first popped.
Operations push, pop, peek and isEmpty are all O(1).
Array stack: top starts at −1; overflow when top == MAX − 1; underflow when top == −1.
Linked stack: the head of a singly linked list is the top.
The call stack stores a frame per function call; infinite recursion causes stack overflow.
Uses: undo/redo, browser back, reversing, backtracking, bracket matching, DFS.
Two stacks can share one array by growing from opposite ends.
lessons.tip: For any stack trace, draw a vertical box and write items bottom to top, crossing out popped items. Keep a separate line for the popped values in order; most exam questions ask for both.
lessons.task: Stack 6 books on a table. Do this sequence: push A, push B, pop, push C, push D, pop, pop. Write down the popped order and the final pile. Then check which of these outputs are possible when pushing 1, 2, 3 in order: 2 3 1 and 3 1 2.

quiz.q: Which principle does a stack follow?
quiz.explain: The most recently pushed item is removed first.

quiz.q: In an array stack with top starting at −1, when does underflow occur?
options: When top == −1 and pop is called
quiz.explain: top == −1 means the stack is empty; popping then is underflow.

quiz.q: After push(5), push(9), pop(), push(3), what is on top?
quiz.explain: 9 is popped, then 3 is pushed on top of 5.

quiz.q: If 1, 2, 3 are pushed in order with pops allowed anytime, which output is impossible?
quiz.explain: If 3 comes out first, 2 is above 1, so 2 must come out before 1.

quiz.q: What does the call stack store for each function call?
options: A frame with parameters, local variables and return address
quiz.explain: Each call pushes an activation record that is popped when the function returns.

lessons.title: Stack Applications: Brackets and Expressions
lessons.content:
When you type 2 + 3 × 4 into a calculator app, it answers 14, not 20. It knows that multiplication comes before addition. But how does a program, reading the symbols one by one from left to right, figure that out? And how does a code editor instantly underline a missing closing bracket in your program? The surprising answer to both questions is the humble stack from the last lesson. This lesson walks through the classic stack applications that appear in almost every data structures exam. Balanced brackets: An expression like {[(a + b) × c] − d} is balanced if every opening bracket has a matching closing bracket of the same type, and they close in the right order. ( [ ) ] is not balanced, even though each type appears twice, because the round bracket closes while the square one is still open. The rule 'last opened must be first closed' is exactly LIFO, so a stack is the natural tool. The bracket algorithm: Scan the expression from left to right. When you see an opening bracket, push it. When you see a closing bracket, if the stack is empty, it is unbalanced (a closing bracket with no partner). Otherwise pop the top and check that it is the matching type; if not, it is unbalanced. Ignore other characters. At the end, the expression is balanced only if the stack is empty; leftover openers mean something was never closed. Time O(n), space O(n) in the worst case. Tracing brackets: Check { ( [ ] ) }. Push {, push (, push [. See ]: pop [, match. See ): pop (, match. See }: pop {, match. Stack empty at the end: balanced. Now check ( [ ) ]. Push (, push [. See ): pop [, which does not match ), so unbalanced, stop. And ( ( ): push (, push (, see ), pop (. End of input, stack still has one (, so unbalanced. Three notations: The way we usually write expressions, with the operator between operands like A + B, is called infix. If the operator comes before the operands, + A B, it is prefix, also called Polish notation after the Polish logician Jan Łukasiewicz. If the operator comes after the operands, A B +, it is postfix, also called reverse Polish notation (RPN). The great thing about prefix and postfix is that they never need brackets and have no precedence rules to remember; the order of symbols alone decides the order of operations. Precedence and associativity: In infix, we need rules. Typical precedence from highest to lowest: brackets, then exponent (^), then × and /, then + and −. Associativity decides the order among equal-precedence operators: + − × / are left-associative, so A − B − C means (A − B) − C. Exponent is usually right-associative, so A ^ B ^ C means A ^ (B ^ C). Both rules matter when converting, so state them in exam answers. Converting by hand: To convert infix to postfix by hand, fully bracket the expression according to the rules, then move each operator to just after its closing bracket, then remove the brackets. A + B × C becomes (A + (B × C)), then A B C × +. For prefix, move each operator to just before its opening bracket: + A × B C. (A + B) × C becomes A B + C × in postfix and × + A B C in prefix. Hand conversion is good for checking your algorithm's answer. Infix to postfix with a stack: Scan the infix expression left to right, using an operator stack and an output list. If the symbol is an operand, append it to the output. If it is '(', push it. If it is ')', pop operators to the output until you pop the matching '(' (discard both brackets). If it is an operator op, pop operators from the stack to the output while the top is an operator with higher precedence than op, or equal precedence and op is left-associative; then push op. At the end, pop all remaining operators to the output. Trace 1: A + B × C − D. Read A: output A. Read +: stack empty, push +. Read B: output A B. Read ×: top is +, lower precedence, so push ×; stack + ×. Read C: output A B C. Read −: top is ×, higher, pop it (output A B C ×); top is +, equal precedence and − is left-associative, pop it (output A B C × +); push −. Read D: output A B C × + D. End: pop −. Final postfix: A B C × + D −. Trace 2 with brackets: (A + B) × (C − D). Read (: push. A: output A. +: top is (, push +. B: output A B. ): pop + to output, pop and discard (. Output A B +. ×: stack empty, push ×. (: push. C: output A B + C. −: top is (, push. D: output A B + C D. ): pop −, discard (. Output A B + C D −. End: pop ×. Final: A B + C D − ×. Right associativity: For A ^ B ^ C, when the second ^ arrives, the top of the stack is ^ with equal precedence, but ^ is right-associative, so we do not pop; we push. At the end we pop both: A B C ^ ^. That means A ^ (B ^ C), which is correct. If you accidentally popped, you would get A B ^ C ^, which means (A ^ B) ^ C, a different value: for 2 ^ 3 ^ 2, the correct answer is 2 ^ 9 = 512, while the wrong one is 8 ^ 2 = 64. Evaluating postfix: This is where postfix shines. Scan left to right with an operand stack. If the symbol is a number, push it. If it is an operator, pop the top value (call it b), pop the next value (call it a), compute a op b, and push the result. At the end, the single value left on the stack is the answer. The order matters: the first popped value is the right operand. For 8 2 /, pop 2 as b, pop 8 as a, compute 8 / 2 = 4. Trace postfix evaluation: Evaluate 6 2 3 + − 3 8 2 / + ×. Push 6, push 2, push 3. +: pop 3 and 2, push 5; stack 6 5. −: pop 5 and 6, push 6 − 5 = 1. Push 3, push 8, push 2; stack 1 3 8 2. /: pop 2 and 8, push 4; stack 1 3 4. +: pop 4 and 3, push 7; stack 1 7. ×: pop 7 and 1, push 7. Answer: 7. Time O(n), and no brackets or precedence were needed at all. Evaluating prefix: For prefix, scan from right to left. Push operands. On an operator, pop the first value as a (the left operand) and the next as b, compute a op b, and push. For − × 2 3 4: from the right, push 4, push 3, push 2. ×: pop 2 (a) and 3 (b), push 6. −: pop 6 (a) and 4 (b), push 2. Answer 2, which matches (2 × 3) − 4. Note that the operand order is the reverse of the postfix case. Infix to prefix: One common method: reverse the infix expression, swapping '(' and ')'; convert that to postfix (with a careful rule for associativity: pop on strictly higher precedence for left-associative operators); then reverse the result. For (A + B) × C: reversed with swapped brackets is C × (B + A); its postfix is C B A + ×; reversed, × + A B C. Some textbooks scan the original from right to left instead; both give the same answer when done carefully. Why computers like postfix: A compiler often turns your infix arithmetic into a postfix-like sequence, because a machine can then evaluate it in a single pass with a stack and no backtracking. The Java Virtual Machine and Python's bytecode are stack-based: to compute a + b × c, they push a, push b, push c, multiply, add. Old HP scientific calculators famously used RPN, and some engineers still swear by them. Real life example 1, a code editor's bracket check: When you write if (marks[i] > 80) { grade = 'A'; } in VS Code, the editor runs the bracket algorithm as you type. Each (, [ and { is pushed, and each closer pops and checks. If you forget a }, the stack is not empty at the end of the file, and the editor highlights the unmatched {. The same algorithm checks matching HTML tags like
and
, where the 'brackets' are tag names. Real life example 2, a shopkeeper's calculator: A shop in Bangabazar uses a billing app. The cashier types 3 × 250 + 2 × 120 − 50. The app converts it to postfix, 3 250 × 2 120 × + 50 −, and evaluates: 750, then 240, then 990, then 940. The final bill is 940 taka. Without precedence handling, the app might compute left to right as ((3 × 250 + 2) × 120) − 50 and overcharge wildly, so the stack algorithm literally protects the customer's wallet. Common mistakes: In postfix evaluation, popping operands in the wrong order, which gives wrong answers for − and /. In conversion, forgetting to pop all operators at the end. Treating ^ as left-associative. Pushing ')' onto the stack. In bracket checking, forgetting to check for an empty stack when a closer arrives, or forgetting that leftover openers at the end mean unbalanced. Mixing up the prefix scanning direction. What exams ask: Write the algorithm to check balanced parentheses and trace it. Convert given infix expressions to postfix and prefix, showing the stack and output at every step in a table. Evaluate a postfix or prefix expression showing the stack. Explain why postfix needs no brackets. The table format, with columns for symbol scanned, stack contents and output, is what examiners expect. A table habit: For conversion questions, draw three columns: 'Symbol', 'Stack' and 'Postfix'. Fill one row per symbol. Examiners can then see each decision, and you can catch your own mistakes, especially at the moments where you pop because of equal precedence. Many students lose marks not because the final answer is wrong, but because no steps are shown. Practice set: Convert A × (B + C) / D to postfix: A B C + × D /. Convert A + B × (C ^ D − E) to postfix: A B C D ^ E − × +. Evaluate 2 3 1 × + 9 −: 3 × 1 = 3, 2 + 3 = 5, 5 − 9 = −4. Check yourself against these before the exam. Recap: A stack checks balanced brackets by pushing openers and matching each closer with the top. Infix needs precedence and associativity rules; prefix and postfix do not need brackets at all. The operator-stack algorithm converts infix to postfix in O(n), and an operand stack evaluates postfix in O(n), popping the right operand first. These techniques sit inside compilers, calculators and code editors you use every day.
key_points: Balanced brackets: push openers, pop and match on closers, stack must be empty at the end.
Infix: A + B; prefix (Polish): + A B; postfix (reverse Polish): A B +.
Prefix and postfix need no brackets or precedence rules.
Infix to postfix: operands go to output; pop higher or equal (left-assoc) precedence operators before pushing.
Exponent is right-associative: A ^ B ^ C becomes A B C ^ ^.
Postfix evaluation: push numbers; on an operator pop b then a, push a op b.
Both conversion and evaluation run in O(n) time.
lessons.tip: Always solve conversion questions in a three-column table (symbol, stack, output). It shows the examiner your steps and catches equal-precedence mistakes.
lessons.task: Convert (5 + 3) × (8 − 2) / 4 to postfix on paper using a table. Then evaluate your postfix with a stack and check that it equals 12.

quiz.q: What is the postfix form of A + B × C?
quiz.explain: × has higher precedence, so B × C is done first: A B C × +.

quiz.q: Evaluate the postfix expression 5 3 + 2 ×.
Why is ( [ ) ] unbalanced?
options: The ) arrives while [ is on top of the stack
quiz.explain: The last opened bracket must close first; ) does not match [.

quiz.q: A ^ B ^ C in postfix (with ^ right-associative) is:
quiz.explain: Right associativity means A ^ (B ^ C), giving A B C ^ ^.

quiz.q: When evaluating postfix, for a − operator you pop b and then a. What do you push?
quiz.explain: The first popped value is the right operand.

lessons.title: Recursion and the Call Stack
lessons.content:
Imagine you are sitting in a cinema hall and you want to know your row number, but it is dark and there are no signs. You tap the person in front and ask, 'What row are you in?'. They do not know either, so they tap the person in front of them and ask the same question. This continues until someone in the very first row says, 'I am in row 1.' Then the answer travels back: the person behind says 'I am in row 2', the next says 'row 3', and finally the answer reaches you. That chain of asking and answering is recursion.

What it is: Recursion is when a function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of the same problem. Every recursive function has two essential parts. The base case is a version of the problem small enough to answer directly, without another call, like the first row in the cinema. The recursive case breaks the problem into a smaller piece and calls the function on that piece, then uses the answer, like 'my row is the row in front plus one'.

Why it matters: Many problems are naturally defined in terms of smaller copies of themselves. A folder contains files and smaller folders. A tree is a root with smaller trees as children. Sorting a list can be done by sorting two halves and merging them. Recursion lets you write such solutions in a few clear lines. In this course, tree traversals, binary search, merge sort, quick sort and depth-first search are all most naturally written recursively.

Factorial: The factorial of n, written n!, is 1 × 2 × 3 × ... × n. Notice that n! = n × (n − 1)!. That gives a recursive definition: fact(n) = 1 if n == 0 (base case), otherwise n × fact(n − 1) (recursive case). fact(4) = 4 × fact(3) = 4 × 3 × fact(2) = 4 × 3 × 2 × fact(1) = 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 × fact(0) = 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 × 1 = 24.

What happens on the call stack: Remember from the stack lesson that each function call pushes a frame. Calling fact(4) pushes a frame with n = 4, which pauses at 'n × fact(n − 1)' and calls fact(3), pushing another frame. The stack grows: fact(4), fact(3), fact(2), fact(1), fact(0). fact(0) hits the base case and returns 1; its frame is popped. fact(1) resumes, computes 1 × 1 = 1, returns, popped. Then fact(2) returns 2, fact(3) returns 6, and fact(4) returns 24. The stack grew to 5 frames and then shrank back to zero.

Winding and unwinding: The phase where calls keep going deeper is called winding; the phase where results come back up is called unwinding. Work done before the recursive call happens on the way down, and work done after it happens on the way up. For example, printDown(n): if n == 0 return; print(n); printDown(n − 1) prints 3 2 1 for n = 3. Moving the print after the call, printUp(n): if n == 0 return; printUp(n − 1); print(n), prints 1 2 3. Same calls, different order of output.

Complexity of recursion: To find the time of a recursive function, write a recurrence. For factorial, T(n) = T(n − 1) + c, because each call does a constant amount of work plus one smaller call. Expanding gives T(n) = c × n + T(0), which is O(n). Space is also O(n), because the call stack holds up to n + 1 frames at once. Always remember that recursion uses stack space even if you never create an array.

Fibonacci, the trap: The Fibonacci sequence is 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, ... where each number is the sum of the previous two: fib(0) = 0, fib(1) = 1, fib(n) = fib(n − 1) + fib(n − 2). The direct recursive code is beautiful but terribly slow. fib(5) calls fib(4) and fib(3); fib(4) calls fib(3) again and fib(2); and so on. fib(3) is computed twice, fib(2) three times. The number of calls grows exponentially, roughly like 1.6^n, so fib(50) by plain recursion would take billions of calls.

Fixing Fibonacci with memoization: The fix is to remember answers. Keep an array memo where memo[k] stores fib(k) once computed. Before computing fib(k), check memo; if it is there, return it. Now each fib(k) is computed only once, so the time becomes O(n). This idea, recursion plus a memory of solved subproblems, is the heart of dynamic programming, which you will study in the Algorithms course. An even simpler fix is a loop that keeps the last two values: O(n) time and O(1) space.

Tower of Hanoi: The most famous recursion puzzle. There are three pegs, A, B and C, and n discs of different sizes stacked on A, largest at the bottom. Move all discs to C, moving one disc at a time and never placing a larger disc on a smaller one. The recursive idea: to move n discs from A to C using B, first move the top n − 1 discs from A to B (using C), then move the largest disc from A to C, then move the n − 1 discs from B to C (using A). Base case: moving 1 disc is a single move.

Hanoi for 3 discs: Following the recipe: move disc 1 A→C, disc 2 A→B, disc 1 C→B (now two discs on B), disc 3 A→C, disc 1 B→A, disc 2 B→C, disc 1 A→C. Seven moves. The number of moves satisfies T(n) = 2T(n − 1) + 1 with T(1) = 1, which gives T(n) = 2^n − 1. For 3 discs that is 7; for 10 discs, 1,023; for 64 discs, about 1.8 × 10^19 moves, which is why the legend says the world ends when the monks finish.

Recursion on arrays and lists: Sum of an array a[0..n−1]: sum(a, n) = 0 if n == 0, else a[n − 1] + sum(a, n − 1). Printing a linked list in reverse: printRev(p): if p == NULL return; printRev(p->next); print(p->data). The recursion goes to the end first, then prints on the way back, so 10 → 20 → 30 prints 30 20 10. Binary search can also be written recursively: search the left or right half by calling itself with a smaller range.

Types of recursion: Direct recursion is when a function calls itself. Indirect recursion is when A calls B and B calls A, for example isEven(n) calls isOdd(n − 1) and isOdd(n) calls isEven(n − 1). Linear recursion makes one recursive call per invocation, like factorial. Tree recursion makes two or more, like Fibonacci and Hanoi. Tail recursion is when the recursive call is the very last thing the function does, with nothing left to compute after it returns.

Tail recursion: Ordinary factorial, return n × fact(n − 1), is not tail recursive, because the multiplication happens after the call returns. A tail-recursive version carries the answer along: factT(n, acc) = acc if n == 0, else factT(n − 1, n × acc), called as factT(4, 1). Some compilers can turn tail calls into a simple loop, so the stack does not grow; this is called tail call optimisation. Many C compilers do this when optimising, but Python and Java generally do not, so deep recursion in those languages can still overflow.

Recursion versus iteration: Anything written recursively can be written with loops, possibly with an explicit stack. Recursion is often shorter and closer to the mathematical definition, especially for trees and divide-and-conquer. Iteration usually uses less memory and avoids function-call overhead and stack overflow. A good rule: use recursion when the problem is naturally recursive (trees, nested structures, divide and conquer) and the depth is reasonable; use loops for simple repetition like summing a list.

Converting recursion to iteration: Because recursion uses the call stack, you can always simulate it with your own stack. For example, an iterative depth-first traversal of a tree pushes nodes onto an explicit stack instead of making recursive calls. This is useful when the recursion depth could be huge, such as a linked list with a million nodes, where the system call stack might overflow but an explicit stack on the heap would not.

Real life example 1, folders on your laptop: To find the total size of a folder, add the sizes of its files, then, for each subfolder, find its total size the same way, and add those too. A folder with no subfolders is the base case. Your operating system does exactly this when you right-click a folder and choose Properties. A program to list every photo on a pen drive, however deeply nested in folders named 'Eid 2024' or 'Cox's Bazar trip', is naturally recursive.

Real life example 2, Russian dolls and family trees: The nesting dolls sold in gift shops each contain a smaller doll, until the tiniest one, which is solid: the base case. Opening them is a recursion. Counting your ancestors works the same way: your ancestors are your parents plus your parents' ancestors. Genealogy apps that draw family trees across generations use recursion to walk from you back to your great-great-grandparents.

Common mistakes: Forgetting the base case, or writing one that is never reached (for example fact(n − 2) when n is odd jumps past 0), which causes infinite recursion and a stack overflow. Not making the problem smaller in the recursive call. Using plain recursion for Fibonacci with large n. Forgetting that recursion uses O(depth) stack space. Mixing up the order of printing before versus after the recursive call.

What exams ask: Define recursion, base case and recursive case. Write recursive functions for factorial, Fibonacci, GCD, sum of digits or power. Trace a recursive call and draw the call stack. Solve the Tower of Hanoi for 3 discs, list the moves, and prove that n discs need 2^n − 1 moves. Compare recursion and iteration. Define tail recursion and give an example. Find the output of a small recursive function.

A tracing question: What does f(3) print? f(n): if n == 0 return; print(n); f(n − 1); print(n). Winding prints 3, 2, 1; unwinding prints 1, 2, 3. Output: 3 2 1 1 2 3. Draw the call stack as you go and this kind of question becomes easy.

GCD, a classic: Euclid's algorithm finds the greatest common divisor recursively: gcd(a, b) = a if b == 0, else gcd(b, a mod b). gcd(48, 18) = gcd(18, 12) = gcd(12, 6) = gcd(6, 0) = 6. It is one of the oldest algorithms known, and it shrinks the numbers so fast that it needs only O(log(min(a, b))) steps.

Recap: Recursion solves a problem by calling itself on smaller versions until reaching a base case. Each call pushes a frame on the call stack; results come back during unwinding. Recursive time is found with recurrences: factorial is O(n), naive Fibonacci is exponential, and Hanoi needs 2^n − 1 moves. Memoization fixes repeated work, tail recursion can be optimised into loops, and any recursion can be rewritten with loops and an explicit stack. Next, we return to linear structures with queues.
key_points: Recursion: a function calls itself on a smaller version of the problem.
Every recursion needs a base case and a recursive case that moves toward it.
Each call pushes a stack frame; deep or infinite recursion causes stack overflow.
Factorial recursion is O(n) time and O(n) stack space.
Naive recursive Fibonacci is exponential; memoization or a loop makes it O(n).
Tower of Hanoi with n discs needs 2^n − 1 moves.
Tail recursion: the recursive call is the last action and can be optimised into a loop.
lessons.tip: When tracing recursion, draw each call as a new box stacked on the previous one, write the parameters inside, and fill in the return value when you cross it out. It turns a confusing tangle into a neat staircase.
lessons.task: Use three cups as pegs and three coins of different sizes as discs. Solve the Tower of Hanoi following the recursive recipe and count your moves; you should get 7. Then try 4 coins and check you need 15.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the base case in recursion?
options: To stop the recursion with a direct answer
quiz.explain: Without a base case, the calls never stop and the stack overflows.

quiz.q: How many moves does the Tower of Hanoi need for 4 discs?
Why is naive recursive Fibonacci slow?
options: It recomputes the same subproblems many times
quiz.explain: fib(k) for small k is recomputed again and again, giving exponential calls.

quiz.q: What does f(2) print? f(n): if n == 0 return; f(n − 1); print(n)
quiz.explain: The print happens during unwinding, so the smaller value prints first.

quiz.q: A function is tail recursive when:
options: The recursive call is the last action, with nothing computed after it
quiz.explain: Nothing remains to do after the call returns, so a compiler can reuse the frame.

lessons.title: Queues: First In, First Out
lessons.content:
Stand in the line at a Sonali Bank counter on salary day. The person who came first is served first, newcomers join at the back, and nobody is allowed to cut into the middle. If someone tried to serve the last person first, there would be a riot. That fair, orderly line is a queue, and computers use exactly the same rule to handle print jobs, network packets, customer requests and much more.

What it is: A queue is a linear data structure where items are inserted at one end, called the rear (or tail), and removed from the other end, called the front (or head). The rule is FIFO: First In, First Out. Adding an item is called enqueue, and removing the front item is called dequeue. We also have peek (or front) to look at the front item without removing it, isEmpty and, for fixed-size queues, isFull.

Stack versus queue: A stack has one open end, so the newest item leaves first (LIFO), like plates. A queue has two ends with different jobs, so the oldest item leaves first (FIFO), like a bank line. That one difference changes everything about where they are used: stacks for undo and backtracking, queues for fairness and processing things in arrival order.

A trace: Start empty. enqueue(10): [10], front = 10, rear = 10. enqueue(20): [10, 20]. enqueue(30): [10, 20, 30]. dequeue() returns 10, leaving [20, 30]. peek() returns 20. enqueue(40): [20, 30, 40]. dequeue() returns 20. dequeue() returns 30. Now only 40 remains. Compare with the stack trace from lesson 9: with the same pushes, a stack would have returned 30 first.

Simple array implementation: Use an array q[MAX] with two indices, front and rear. Start with front = 0 and rear = −1 (empty). enqueue(x): if rear == MAX − 1, overflow; else rear = rear + 1; q[rear] = x. dequeue(): if front > rear, underflow; else x = q[front]; front = front + 1; return x. Both are O(1). The number of items is rear − front + 1.

The problem with the simple array queue: Suppose MAX = 5. Enqueue 5 items: rear = 4. Dequeue 3 items: front = 3. Now the queue holds only 2 items, and boxes 0, 1 and 2 are empty. But enqueue reports overflow, because rear == MAX − 1. The free space at the front is wasted. One bad fix is to shift all items to the front after each dequeue, but that makes dequeue O(n). The good fix is the circular queue.

Circular queue: Imagine the array bent into a ring, so that after the last box comes box 0 again. When rear reaches the end, it wraps around to the beginning, reusing the freed space. The wrap-around is done with the modulo operator: rear = (rear + 1) % MAX, and front = (front + 1) % MAX. Everything stays O(1), and no space is wasted.

Full or empty? With a ring, the tricky part is telling a full queue from an empty one, because in both cases front and rear can end up in similar positions. A common approach keeps a count of items: empty when count == 0, full when count == MAX. Another classic approach, found in many textbooks, leaves one slot always unused: the queue is empty when front == rear and full when (rear + 1) % MAX == front. In that version, an array of size MAX can hold at most MAX − 1 items.

Circular queue code (count version): enqueue(x): if count == MAX, overflow; rear = (rear + 1) % MAX; q[rear] = x; count = count + 1. dequeue(): if count == 0, underflow; x = q[front]; front = (front + 1) % MAX; count = count − 1; return x. Start with front = 0, rear = MAX − 1, count = 0, so the first enqueue puts the item at index 0.

Circular trace with MAX = 4: enqueue A, B, C: positions 0, 1, 2; front = 0, rear = 2, count 3. dequeue returns A; front = 1, count 2. dequeue returns B; front = 2, count 1. enqueue D: rear = 3. enqueue E: rear = (3 + 1) % 4 = 0, so E goes into index 0, reusing A's old box. enqueue F: rear = 1, count 4, full. Order of items from front: C, D, E, F. The ring reused the space at the start without moving anything.

Linked list implementation: Use a singly linked list with two pointers: front pointing to the first node and rear pointing to the last. enqueue(x): create node n with next = NULL; if rear == NULL (empty), front = rear = n; else rear->next = n; rear = n. dequeue(): if front == NULL, underflow; t = front; x = t->data; front = front->next; if front == NULL, rear = NULL; free(t); return x. Both O(1). Notice that we insert at the tail and delete at the head, which is exactly where a singly linked list with a tail pointer is fast.

Why not dequeue from the tail? In a singly linked list, deleting the last node is O(n), as we saw in lesson 7. So we always enqueue at the rear and dequeue at the front. If you reversed that, dequeue would become slow. Choosing which end does what is a small design decision with a big effect.

Queue using two stacks: A classic interview puzzle. Keep an inbox stack and an outbox stack. enqueue pushes onto inbox. dequeue pops from outbox; if outbox is empty, first pop everything from inbox and push it onto outbox, which reverses the order so the oldest item ends up on top. Each item is moved at most twice in its lifetime, so dequeue is O(1) amortized, using the same idea as dynamic arrays.

Applications in computing: Printers keep a print queue: documents are printed in the order they were sent. Operating systems keep a ready queue of processes waiting for the CPU. Routers queue network packets. Web servers queue incoming requests. Keyboards buffer keystrokes in a queue so letters appear in the order you typed them, even if the computer is briefly busy. Breadth-first search on trees and graphs uses a queue to visit nodes level by level, as we will see later.

Buffers between fast and slow: When a fast producer sends data to a slow consumer, a queue in the middle smooths things out. When you stream a cricket match on Toffee, video chunks arrive from the internet into a buffer queue, and the player removes them in order to display them. If the network is briefly slow, the player keeps playing from the queue. If the queue empties, you see the dreaded buffering circle.

Real life example 1, the token system at a passport office: At the passport office in Agargaon, you take a token number. The screen calls tokens in increasing order. The token machine is an enqueue; the display calling 'Token 147, counter 3' is a dequeue. Because the tokens are served strictly in the order issued, nobody can jump ahead, which is exactly the fairness that FIFO guarantees. If the system used a stack, the newest arrival would be served first, which would be absurd.

Real life example 2, ride requests on Pathao: When many people in Dhanmondi request a ride at the same time, requests enter a queue to be matched with drivers. Real systems also consider distance and priority, but the basic idea is that requests are processed in arrival order rather than randomly, so nobody waits forever. When the queue grows too long during rain or Eid rush, the app shows longer waiting times, because the queue length tells you how much work is ahead.

Real life example 3, the print queue in a computer lab: In a university lab, 30 students send assignments to one printer just before the deadline. The printer cannot print them all at once, so the jobs wait in a queue. The first student to click print gets their pages first. A student can cancel their own job, which removes it from the queue, but cannot move it ahead of others.

Common mistakes: Confusing FIFO with LIFO. In the simple array queue, forgetting that space at the front is wasted. In the circular queue, forgetting the modulo and running past the end of the array. Mixing up the full and empty conditions, especially in the 'one slot empty' version. In the linked version, forgetting to set rear = NULL when the last item is dequeued, leaving rear pointing to freed memory.

What exams ask: Define a queue and its operations. Write enqueue and dequeue for array, circular and linked implementations with overflow and underflow checks. Explain why a circular queue is better than a simple array queue. Trace a sequence of operations on a circular queue of a given size, showing front, rear and contents. Implement a queue using two stacks. Compare stacks and queues.

A typical exam trace: 'A circular queue of size 5 uses the one-empty-slot rule, with front = rear = 0 initially. Show front and rear after: enqueue 1, 2, 3, dequeue, enqueue 4, 5.' With this rule, enqueue does rear = (rear + 1) % 5 then stores, and dequeue does front = (front + 1) % 5 then reads. After three enqueues, rear = 3. Dequeue: front = 1. Enqueue 4: rear = 4. Enqueue 5: rear = 0. Is it full? Full means (rear + 1) % 5 == front, and (0 + 1) % 5 = 1 = front, so yes, full with 4 items. Different textbooks use slightly different conventions, so always state yours.

Queues in real libraries: In Python, collections.deque gives O(1) append and popleft, and is the usual queue; using a plain list with pop(0) is a common beginner mistake, because removing the first element shifts all the others and costs O(n). In Java, the Queue interface is often used with ArrayDeque or LinkedList, with offer to enqueue and poll to dequeue. In C++, std::queue wraps a deque underneath. Inside, most of these use a circular buffer or a chain of blocks, exactly the ideas in this lesson.

Queue length and waiting time: There is a neat rule from queueing theory called Little's Law: on average, the number of items in a system equals the arrival rate times the average time each item spends in it. If 10 customers arrive per minute at a bKash agent point and each spends 3 minutes there, about 30 customers are inside on average. Engineers use this kind of reasoning to decide how many servers or counters a system needs.

Recap: A queue inserts at the rear and removes from the front, following FIFO. Enqueue, dequeue and peek are O(1). A simple array queue wastes space, so we use a circular queue with modulo arithmetic, distinguishing full from empty by a count or by keeping one slot free. A linked queue keeps front and rear pointers. Queues give fairness and order to printers, CPUs, networks, streaming and breadth-first search. Next, we look at queues with extra powers: deques and priority queues.
key_points: A queue is FIFO: insert (enqueue) at the rear, remove (dequeue) at the front.
Enqueue, dequeue and peek are O(1).
A simple array queue wastes space at the front after dequeues.
A circular queue wraps indices with modulo: rear = (rear + 1) % MAX.
Tell full from empty with a count, or by keeping one slot unused.
Linked queue: enqueue at the tail, dequeue at the head; reset rear when it becomes empty.
Uses: print queues, CPU scheduling, network buffers, streaming, BFS.
lessons.tip: For circular queue traces, draw the array as a circle of numbered boxes and move two coloured arrows (front and rear) around it. Seeing the wrap-around makes the modulo obvious.
lessons.task: Draw a circle with 5 boxes numbered 0 to 4. Using the count method, perform: enqueue A, B, C, D; dequeue twice; enqueue E, F, G. Write front, rear and count after every step, and list the final queue from front to rear.

quiz.q: Which principle does a queue follow?
quiz.explain: The earliest inserted item leaves first.

quiz.q: After enqueue(1), enqueue(2), enqueue(3), dequeue(), what is at the front?
quiz.explain: 1 is removed, so 2 becomes the front.

quiz.q: In a circular queue of size MAX, how is rear advanced?
quiz.explain: Modulo makes the index wrap around to 0 after the last box.

quiz.q: What is the main problem of a simple (non-circular) array queue?
options: Space freed at the front cannot be reused
quiz.explain: rear reaches the end even when the front boxes are empty.

quiz.q: In a linked list queue, why do we dequeue at the head rather than the tail?
options: Deleting the head is O(1) while deleting the tail of a singly linked list is O(n)
quiz.explain: Removing the last node needs its predecessor, which requires a walk.

lessons.title: Deques and Priority Queues
lessons.content:
Think about a hospital emergency room in Dhaka Medical College. Patients arrive one after another, but the doctor does not simply call them in arrival order. A child with a high fever waits, while a road accident victim who arrived later is rushed in first. The line is ordered by how urgent each case is, not by when people came. Now think about a local bus where people can get on and off from both the front door and the back door. Those two pictures are the priority queue and the deque, two powerful cousins of the ordinary queue.

The deque, what it is: A deque (pronounced 'deck'), short for double-ended queue, is a linear structure where you can insert and delete at both ends. The operations are insertFront, insertRear, deleteFront and deleteRear, plus peekFront and peekRear. A deque can behave like a stack (use only one end) or like a queue (insert at one end, delete at the other), so it is a generalisation of both.

A deque trace: Start empty. insertRear(10): [10]. insertRear(20): [10, 20]. insertFront(5): [5, 10, 20]. deleteRear() returns 20: [5, 10]. insertFront(1): [1, 5, 10]. deleteFront() returns 1: [5, 10]. Every operation touched only an end, and each one is O(1) with a good implementation.

Restricted deques: Two special kinds often appear in exams. An input-restricted deque allows insertion at only one end (say the rear) but deletion at both ends. An output-restricted deque allows deletion at only one end (say the front) but insertion at both ends. They sit between a full deque and a plain queue, and exam questions sometimes ask which output orders are possible with each kind.

Implementing a deque with a circular array: Use the same ring idea as the circular queue. insertRear moves rear forward: rear = (rear + 1) % MAX. deleteFront moves front forward: front = (front + 1) % MAX. The new parts move backwards: insertFront does front = (front − 1 + MAX) % MAX, and deleteRear does rear = (rear − 1 + MAX) % MAX. The '+ MAX' prevents a negative index, because in C the % of a negative number can be negative. Keep a count to tell full from empty. All operations are O(1).

Implementing a deque with a doubly linked list: Keep head and tail pointers. Inserting or deleting at either end is O(1), because each node knows both neighbours. This is exactly the situation where a doubly linked list beats a singly linked one: with a singly linked list, deleteRear would be O(n). Real libraries such as Python's collections.deque use a chain of fixed-size blocks, which combines the benefits of arrays and links.

Deque applications: Checking a palindrome: put all characters in a deque, then repeatedly remove one from each end and compare. The sliding window maximum problem, finding the largest value in every window of k consecutive numbers, is solved in O(n) with a deque that keeps candidate indices in decreasing order of value. Undo histories with a size limit use a deque: new actions go on one end, and when the limit is reached the oldest action falls off the other end. Some work-stealing schedulers let a thread take work from the back of another thread's deque.

The priority queue, what it is: A priority queue is an ADT where every item has a priority, and the item removed next is always the one with the highest priority (in a max-priority queue) or the lowest key (in a min-priority queue), regardless of arrival order. The main operations are insert(item, priority), extractMax (or extractMin) which removes and returns the top-priority item, and peekMax which just looks at it. Some versions also offer increaseKey or decreaseKey to change an item's priority.

Priority queue is an ADT, not one structure: This is an important exam point. 'Priority queue' describes behaviour. It can be implemented in several ways, with different costs. The most popular implementation is the binary heap, which we study properly in lesson 18. Here we compare the simple options so you understand why heaps are worth learning.

Option 1, unsorted array or list: insert just appends at the end: O(1). extractMax must scan every item to find the largest, then remove it: O(n). Good if you insert a lot and rarely extract. For example, inserting priorities 4, 9, 2 is instant, but extracting means comparing all three to find 9.

Option 2, sorted array or sorted linked list: Keep items in order of priority. extractMax just takes the item at the high-priority end: O(1) (for an array, keep the largest at the end so removal needs no shifting). But insert must find the right place and, for an array, shift items: O(n). Good if you extract a lot and insert rarely. Inserting 7 into [2, 4, 9] means finding the spot between 4 and 9 and shifting 9.

Option 3, binary heap: A heap keeps items in a special tree shape stored in an array, where the top is always the maximum. Both insert and extractMax take O(log n), and peekMax is O(1). For n = 1,000,000, log₂ n is about 20, so each operation takes around 20 steps instead of up to a million. That balance is why heaps are the standard choice; we will build one in lesson 18.

Option 4, an array of queues: If there are only a few priority levels, say 1 to 5, keep one ordinary FIFO queue per level. insert goes into the queue for its level: O(1). extract checks levels from highest to lowest and dequeues from the first non-empty queue: O(number of levels), which is effectively O(1) if levels are few. Items with the same priority are served in arrival order, which is often exactly what you want, like 'emergency first, then first come first served'.

Ties and stability: When two items have the same priority, which comes first? A plain heap does not guarantee arrival order among equal priorities. If fairness matters, you can store a pair (priority, arrival number) and compare by priority first and arrival number second. This trick turns any priority queue into a stable one.

Priority queue applications in computing: Operating systems schedule processes by priority, so a system process runs before a background update. Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm, which powers map routing, repeatedly extracts the closest unvisited place from a min-priority queue. Huffman coding, used in file compression, repeatedly extracts the two least frequent symbols. Event-driven simulations extract the next event by earliest time. Bandwidth management in routers can send voice call packets before ordinary downloads.

Real life example 1, hospital triage: In an emergency department, each arriving patient gets a triage level, from 1 (immediate) to 5 (non-urgent). The staff use an array-of-queues priority queue: level 1 patients are seen first, and within the same level, earlier arrivals go first. A heart attack patient who arrives at 10:30 is seen before a sprained ankle that arrived at 9:00. This is exactly extractMax with ties broken by arrival.

Real life example 2, Eid travel on a launch terminal: At Sadarghat before Eid, a launch company manages its booking requests. Cabin bookings paid in advance get higher priority than deck tickets bought on the spot, and staff serve the highest priority first. Meanwhile, the gangway onto the launch behaves like a deque during loading and unloading: porters can push goods on from the front and passengers can get off from the back, both ends active at once.

Real life example 3, the 'previous and next' of a video playlist with limited history: A video app keeps your last 50 watched videos. Each new video is added at the front of a deque; when there are more than 50, the oldest is dropped from the back. Pressing 'continue watching' peeks at the front. Both ends are busy, so a deque fits better than a plain queue or stack.

Common mistakes: Thinking a priority queue is FIFO; it is not, priority decides. Saying 'priority queue = heap'; a heap is one implementation of the priority queue ADT. Forgetting the + MAX when moving an index backwards in a circular deque. Mixing up input-restricted (one insertion end) and output-restricted (one deletion end). Assuming equal priorities come out in arrival order with a heap.

What exams ask: Define a deque and its four operations; explain input-restricted and output-restricted deques. Implement a deque using a circular array or doubly linked list. Define a priority queue and give applications. Compare implementations of a priority queue (unsorted array, sorted array, linked list, heap) in a table of insert and delete costs. Trace operations on a deque or a priority queue.

Comparison table to remember: Unsorted array: insert O(1), extractMax O(n). Sorted array: insert O(n), extractMax O(1). Sorted linked list: insert O(n), extractMax O(1). Binary heap: insert O(log n), extractMax O(log n), peek O(1). Array of k FIFO queues: insert O(1), extract O(k). Writing this table neatly is worth full marks in many exams.

Choosing between them: There is no single winner, so look at your numbers first. If n is small, say under 50, even the unsorted array is fine and simplest. If priorities come from a small fixed set, the array of queues is fast and keeps arrival order. If n is large and priorities are arbitrary numbers, use a binary heap. If you also need to remove arbitrary items or change priorities often, look at more advanced structures, which you will meet in the Algorithms course.

A priority queue trace: Use a max-priority queue and insert jobs with priorities: A(3), B(7), C(5), D(7). extractMax returns one of the priority-7 jobs, B or D, depending on how ties are broken; with the (priority, arrival) trick it is B, because B arrived first. Then extractMax returns D, then C(5), then A(3). Notice that A, the very first job, comes out last. That is the opposite of fairness in a plain queue, and it is exactly what we want when urgency matters more than waiting time.

Starvation and ageing: One danger of strict priority is starvation: a low-priority item may wait forever if higher-priority items keep arriving. Operating systems solve this with ageing, slowly increasing the priority of items the longer they wait. After enough time, even the lowest task climbs high enough to be served. It is a small rule that keeps a priority-based system fair in the long run.

Recap: A deque lets you insert and delete at both ends in O(1), using a circular array or a doubly linked list, and generalises both stacks and queues. A priority queue always removes the highest-priority item, regardless of arrival. It is an ADT that can be implemented with unsorted or sorted arrays and lists, multiple FIFO queues, or, most commonly, a binary heap with O(log n) insert and extract. Next, we leave linear structures behind and climb into trees.
key_points: A deque (double-ended queue) allows insertion and deletion at both ends in O(1).
Input-restricted deque: insert at one end only; output-restricted: delete at one end only.
Circular deque moves backward with (i − 1 + MAX) % MAX.
A priority queue removes the highest (or lowest) priority item, not the oldest.
Priority queue is an ADT; heaps, arrays, lists or arrays of queues can implement it.
Unsorted array: O(1) insert, O(n) extract; sorted: O(n) insert, O(1) extract; heap: O(log n) both.
Uses: CPU scheduling, Dijkstra, Huffman coding, triage, sliding-window problems.
lessons.tip: Make one comparison table for all priority queue implementations and keep it on the first page of your notes. Half the priority queue questions are just this table in disguise.
lessons.task: Write 8 tasks for tomorrow on paper slips with a priority from 1 to 3. Put them into three piles (one queue per priority) in the order you wrote them. Now 'extract' them one by one and see the order you would do them.

quiz.q: Which operations does a deque support?
options: Insert and delete only at the rear
Insert and delete at both ends
quiz.explain: Double-ended means both ends allow insertion and deletion.

quiz.q: In an output-restricted deque:
options: Deletion is allowed at only one end
Insertion is allowed at only one end
Only the middle can be accessed
quiz.explain: Output (deletion) is restricted to one end; insertion is allowed at both.

quiz.q: With a binary heap, insert and extractMax in a priority queue take:
quiz.explain: Both operations travel along one path of a balanced tree.

quiz.q: Which statement is correct?
options: A priority queue is always FIFO
A priority queue must be a sorted array
A deque cannot act as a stack
A heap is one way to implement the priority queue ADT
quiz.explain: Priority queue is the behaviour; a heap is a popular implementation.

quiz.q: In a circular-array deque of size MAX, how does insertFront move front?
quiz.explain: Moving backwards needs + MAX to avoid a negative index.

lessons.title: Trees and Binary Trees
lessons.content:
Open the 'This PC' window on your computer. Inside the C drive you find folders like Users and Program Files. Inside Users there is a folder with your name, and inside that, Documents, Downloads and Pictures. Inside Pictures, there might be 'Eid 2025' and 'Sylhet trip'. Every folder has exactly one parent folder, except the drive itself, and any folder can have many children. That shape, branching out from one top point, is a tree, and it is the first non-linear structure in this course.

What a tree is: A tree is a collection of nodes connected by edges, with one special node called the root, such that every other node has exactly one parent, and there are no cycles (you can never walk in a loop and come back to where you started). Formally, a tree is either empty, or a root node together with zero or more subtrees, each of which is itself a tree. That recursive definition is why recursion and trees go together so naturally.

Why trees matter: Lists force everything into one line, so finding something can take O(n). Trees let us branch, and a well-shaped tree with n nodes can have height around log₂ n, so we can reach any node in about log n steps. File systems, the HTML structure of every web page (the DOM), organisation charts, family trees, decision-making in games and AI, database indexes and compilers' expression trees are all trees.

Basic terminology, part 1: The root is the topmost node, with no parent. An edge connects a parent to a child. A node with no children is a leaf (also called an external or terminal node). A node with at least one child is an internal node. Nodes with the same parent are siblings. The ancestors of a node are all nodes on the path from it up to the root; its descendants are all nodes below it. A subtree is a node together with all its descendants.

Basic terminology, part 2: The degree of a node is the number of children it has; the degree of a tree is the maximum degree of any node. The depth of a node is the number of edges from the root to it, so the root has depth 0. The level of a node is usually the same as its depth (some books start levels at 1, so always state your convention). The height of a node is the number of edges on the longest path from it down to a leaf; the height of the tree is the height of the root. A tree with only one node has height 0 under this convention.

A small example: Let A be the root with children B and C. B has children D and E. C has one child F. Then leaves are D, E and F. Internal nodes are A, B and C. Siblings: B and C; D and E. Depth of E is 2. Height of the tree is 2. Degree of B is 2, degree of C is 1, so the degree of the tree is 2. Ancestors of F are C and A. A tree with n nodes always has exactly n − 1 edges, here 6 nodes and 5 edges, because every node except the root has exactly one edge to its parent.

Binary tree: A binary tree is a tree where every node has at most two children, called the left child and the right child. Left and right matter: a node with only a left child is a different binary tree from a node with only a right child. In C: struct TreeNode { int data; struct TreeNode *left; struct TreeNode *right; };. A missing child is NULL. Binary trees are the most studied trees because they are simple yet powerful.

Types of binary trees: A full (or strict, or proper) binary tree is one where every node has either 0 or 2 children, never exactly 1. A perfect binary tree is full and also has all leaves at the same depth, so every level is completely filled. A complete binary tree has every level completely filled except possibly the last, and the last level's nodes are as far left as possible. A skewed binary tree is one where every node has only one child, all left (left-skewed) or all right (right-skewed), so it looks like a linked list. Note that some textbooks use 'full' to mean what we call perfect, so read definitions carefully in your exam paper.

Property 1, maximum nodes per level: At level i (root at level 0), a binary tree can have at most 2^i nodes, because each level can at most double. Level 0 has 1, level 1 has 2, level 2 has 4, level 3 has 8.

Property 2, maximum nodes for a given height: A binary tree of height h can have at most 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + 2^h = 2^(h + 1) − 1 nodes. A perfect binary tree of height 3 has 15 nodes. Turned around, a binary tree with n nodes has height at least ⌈log₂(n + 1)⌉ − 1. For n = 15, that minimum height is 3. And the maximum height, for a skewed tree, is n − 1. So the same 15 values could make a tree of height 3 or height 14, which is the key to everything in the next few lessons.

Property 3, leaves and two-child nodes: In any non-empty binary tree, if n₀ is the number of leaves and n₂ the number of nodes with two children, then n₀ = n₂ + 1. Check it on a perfect tree of height 2: 4 leaves and 3 nodes with two children, and 4 = 3 + 1. This neat fact comes up in exam proofs. The proof counts edges two ways: n − 1 edges, and also n₁ + 2n₂ edges coming out of parents, where n = n₀ + n₁ + n₂.

Counting shapes: How many different binary tree shapes are there with n nodes? For n = 1 there is 1, for n = 2 there are 2, for n = 3 there are 5. In general the number is the Catalan number C(n) = (2n)! / ((n + 1)! × n!). For n = 4 it is 14. You are not usually asked to derive it, but the number for n = 3 is a common short question.

Linked representation: Each node is a struct with data, a left pointer and a right pointer, and we keep a pointer to the root. This is flexible: the tree can have any shape, and nodes are added or removed by changing pointers.
