The cost is two pointers per node; in a tree with n nodes, there are 2n pointer fields, of which only n − 1 are used, so n + 1 are NULL. That waste is the motivation for threaded binary trees, which reuse those NULL fields to point to inorder predecessors and successors.

Array representation: Store the tree level by level in an array. With 0-based indexing, the root is at index 0; for a node at index i, its left child is at 2i + 1, its right child at 2i + 2, and its parent at ⌊(i − 1) / 2⌋. With 1-based indexing, the root is at 1, children at 2i and 2i + 1, and parent at ⌊i / 2⌋. No pointers are stored at all; positions alone describe the shape.

When arrays work well: The array form is perfect for complete binary trees, because there are no gaps; the n nodes fill indices 0 to n − 1. That is why heaps, which are complete binary trees, are stored in arrays. For a skewed tree it is terrible: a right-skewed tree of height h needs an array of size 2^(h + 1) − 1 but uses only h + 1 cells. A right-skewed tree with 20 nodes would need over a million slots.

Example of array representation: Take the tree with root 50, children 30 and 70, and 30's children 20 and 40, and 70's left child 60. 0-based array: [50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60]. Check: left of 30 (index 1) is index 3, 20; right is index 4, 40. Left of 70 (index 2) is index 5, 60. Parent of 60 (index 5) is ⌊4 / 2⌋ = 2, which is 70. Everything matches, and because the tree is complete there are no gaps.

General trees as binary trees: A general tree, where a node may have any number of children, can be converted into a binary tree using the left-child right-sibling representation. Each node keeps two pointers: one to its first (leftmost) child and one to its next sibling. A node with five children no longer needs five pointer fields, just two. This is how many systems store trees whose nodes have a variable number of children, like folders.

Forests: A forest is a collection of separate trees. If you delete the root of a tree, its subtrees become a forest. Forests appear in algorithms like disjoint-set union, which is used to group things into connected clusters, and some textbooks convert whole forests into a single binary tree with the same left-child right-sibling trick.

Real life example 1, a cricket tournament bracket: In a knockout tournament with 8 teams, the final is the root, the two semi-finals are its children, the four quarter-finals are below them, and the eight teams are the leaves. It is a perfect binary tree of height 3 with 15 nodes, and the number of matches played is the number of internal nodes, 7. Because n₀ = n₂ + 1, a knockout with t teams always needs t − 1 matches, a fun fact you can check at the next Bangladesh school tournament.

Real life example 2, the HTML of a web page: When your browser opens a Daraz product page, it reads the HTML and builds a tree called the DOM. The html element is the root, with head and body as children; body contains div elements, which contain images, prices and buttons. JavaScript finds the 'Add to Cart' button by walking this tree. Every web page you have ever seen was a tree first.

Real life example 3, an organisation chart: A company like Grameenphone has a CEO at the root, chief officers as children, and department heads, managers and team members below. Asking 'who does this engineer ultimately report to?' means walking up through ancestors. Asking 'how many people are in the marketing division?' means counting all nodes in a subtree.

Common mistakes: Mixing up depth and height. Forgetting that left and right matter in a binary tree. Confusing full, complete and perfect binary trees. Starting levels at 1 in one part of an answer and at 0 in another. Using the 1-based child formula with a 0-based array. Thinking every tree has height about log n; a skewed tree has height n − 1.

What exams ask: Define root, leaf, degree, depth, height, level, sibling, ancestor. Identify these in a given diagram. Define and draw full, complete, perfect and skewed binary trees. Prove that a binary tree has at most 2^i nodes at level i and at most 2^(h + 1) − 1 nodes in total, or that n₀ = n₂ + 1. Show the array and linked representations of a given tree, and explain why the array form suits complete trees.

Recap: A tree is a hierarchy of nodes with one root, no cycles and exactly n − 1 edges. Learn the vocabulary: parent, child, leaf, sibling, ancestor, descendant, degree, depth, level and height. A binary tree gives each node at most a left and a right child. Full, perfect, complete and skewed trees are special shapes. Height ranges from about log₂ n to n − 1. Trees can be stored with pointers or, for complete trees, neatly in an array with 2i + 1 and 2i + 2. Next, we learn to visit every node of a binary tree in four classic orders.
key_points: A tree has one root, every other node has exactly one parent, there are no cycles, and n nodes have n − 1 edges.
Depth counts edges from the root; height counts edges down to the deepest leaf.
A binary tree node has at most two children: left and right.
Full: 0 or 2 children; perfect: full with all leaves at one level; complete: filled left to right.
At most 2^i nodes at level i; at most 2^(h + 1) − 1 nodes for height h; n₀ = n₂ + 1.
Array form (0-based): children at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, parent at ⌊(i − 1)/2⌋; ideal for complete trees.
Left-child right-sibling turns any general tree into a binary tree.
lessons.tip: For every tree question, first write down your convention: does the root have depth 0 or level 1? Height in edges or nodes? Many 'wrong' answers are only wrong because the convention changed halfway.
lessons.task: Draw your own family tree for three generations. Mark the root, leaves, siblings, the depth of each person and the height of the tree. Then write it as a 0-based array, treating the first two children of each person as left and right.

quiz.q: A tree has 12 nodes. How many edges does it have?
quiz.explain: Every node except the root has exactly one edge to its parent: n − 1.

quiz.q: What is the maximum number of nodes in a binary tree of height 3 (root at height 0)?
In a 0-based array representation, where is the right child of the node at index 4?
quiz.explain: Right child is at 2i + 2 = 10.

quiz.q: A binary tree has 9 nodes with two children. How many leaves does it have?
Which binary tree has every level full except possibly the last, filled from the left?
quiz.explain: That is the definition of a complete binary tree.

lessons.title: Binary Tree Traversals
lessons.content:
Imagine you are a new school inspector visiting a school organised like a tree: the headmaster at the top, two assistant heads below, and class teachers under each assistant. You must meet everyone exactly once. You could meet each boss before their team, or after their team, or meet the left team, then the boss, then the right team, or simply go floor by floor. Each plan visits the same people in a different order. Those plans are the four classic tree traversals, and choosing the right one solves a surprising number of problems.

What a traversal is: A traversal visits every node of a tree exactly once in a systematic order. In a linear list there is only one natural order, front to back. In a binary tree, at every node we must decide when to process the node itself (call it N) compared to its left subtree (L) and right subtree (R). By convention we always do L before R, which leaves three depth-first orders, NLR, LNR and LRN, plus one breadth-first order, level by level.

Our example tree: We will use the same tree throughout. The root is A. A's left child is B and right child is C. B has left child D and right child E. C has only a right child, F. Draw it now on paper: A at the top, B and C below, D and E under B, and F under C on the right side. Every traversal below refers to this picture.

Preorder (N L R): Visit the node first, then traverse the left subtree in preorder, then the right subtree in preorder. preorder(t): if t == NULL return; visit(t); preorder(t->left); preorder(t->right). For our tree: visit A, then go left to B: visit B, then D, then E; then go right to C: visit C, then its right child F. Result: A B D E C F. Preorder is useful for copying a tree, because you create each parent before its children, and for printing a folder structure top-down.

Inorder (L N R): Traverse the left subtree, then visit the node, then traverse the right subtree. inorder(t): if t == NULL return; inorder(t->left); visit(t); inorder(t->right). For our tree: from A go left to B, from B go left to D: D has no left child, so visit D; back to B, visit B; then B's right, visit E; back to A, visit A; then go right to C: C has no left child, visit C; then visit F. Result: D B E A C F. In a binary search tree, which we study next, inorder visits the values in sorted order, a famous and very useful fact.

Postorder (L R N): Traverse the left subtree, then the right subtree, then visit the node. postorder(t): if t == NULL return; postorder(t->left); postorder(t->right); visit(t). For our tree: D, E, then B; then on the right, F, then C; finally A. Result: D E B F C A. Postorder handles children before parents, so it is the right order for deleting a tree (free children before the parent) and for computing things like folder sizes, where a parent's size depends on its children's sizes.

A finger trick: To get the three orders quickly by hand, draw a line hugging the tree, starting left of the root and going counter-clockwise around every node. Each node is passed three times: on its left side, below it, and on its right side. Writing the node when you pass its left side gives preorder; when you pass under it gives inorder; when you pass its right side gives postorder. Many students use this to double-check their answers in exams.

Level order (breadth-first): Visit nodes level by level, left to right. For our tree: A, then B C, then D E F. Result: A B C D E F. This cannot be done with simple recursion; it uses a queue. Start by enqueuing the root. Repeat while the queue is not empty: dequeue a node, visit it, then enqueue its left child and right child if they exist. Trace: queue [A]; visit A, enqueue B, C; visit B, enqueue D, E; visit C, enqueue F; visit D; visit E; visit F. Level order is used for printing a tree level by level and for finding the shortest path in unweighted structures.

Complexity: Each traversal visits every node once and does a constant amount of work per node, so time is O(n). The recursive depth-first traversals use the call stack, so their extra space is O(h), where h is the height: O(log n) for a balanced tree, but O(n) for a skewed tree. Level order uses a queue that can hold a whole level at once, which can be about n/2 nodes for a perfect tree, so O(n) space in the worst case.

Iterative inorder with a stack: Recursion can be replaced with an explicit stack. Set cur = root. Loop: while cur is not NULL, push cur and go left (cur = cur->left). When cur is NULL, if the stack is empty, stop; otherwise pop a node, visit it, and set cur = node->right. On our tree: push A, B, D; pop and visit D; D's right is NULL; pop and visit B; go to E, push E; pop and visit E; pop and visit A; go to C, push C; pop and visit C; go to F, push F; pop and visit F. Output D B E A C F, matching the recursive version.

Iterative preorder: Push the root. While the stack is not empty: pop a node and visit it; push its right child, then its left child (so the left one is on top and comes out first). For our tree the output is A B D E C F. Iterative versions matter when the tree might be very deep, because they avoid stack overflow from deep recursion.

Rebuilding a tree from traversals: Given preorder A B D E C F and inorder D B E A C F, can we draw the tree? Yes. The first preorder item, A, is the root. Find A in the inorder list: everything to its left (D B E) is the left subtree, and everything to its right (C F) is the right subtree. Now recurse: the next preorder items for the left part are B D E, so B is the left subtree's root, with D on its left and E on its right in inorder. For the right part, preorder C F and inorder C F: C is the root and F comes after it in inorder, so F is C's right child. We get our original tree back.

Which pairs work: Inorder together with either preorder or postorder uniquely determines a binary tree (assuming all values are distinct). With postorder, the root is the last item instead of the first. But preorder with postorder alone is not enough in general: for example, a root A with a single child B gives preorder A B and postorder B A, whether B is the left or the right child. It works only for full binary trees, where every node has 0 or 2 children. This is a popular theory question.

Expression trees: An arithmetic expression can be stored as a binary tree: operators are internal nodes and operands are leaves. (a + b) × (c − d) becomes a tree with × at the root, a + node on the left with children a and b, and a − node on the right with children c and d. Its preorder is × + a b − c d, which is the prefix expression; its postorder is a b + c d − ×, the postfix expression; and its inorder is a + b × c − d, the infix form, which needs brackets added back to be correct. So the three traversals connect directly to the three notations from lesson 10.

Building an expression tree from postfix: Scan the postfix left to right with a stack of tree pointers. For an operand, create a leaf and push it. For an operator, pop two subtrees (the first popped is the right child), create an operator node with them as children, and push it. At the end, the single tree on the stack is the expression tree. Evaluating the expression is then a postorder traversal: evaluate left, evaluate right, apply the operator.

Useful recursive functions: Count the nodes: count(t) = 0 if t is NULL, else 1 + count(t->left) + count(t->right). Count leaves: if t is NULL return 0; if both children are NULL return 1; else return leaves(left) + leaves(right). Height (in edges): height(NULL) = −1, height(t) = 1 + max(height(left), height(right)). Sum of all values, maximum value, mirror image (swap left and right at every node) all follow the same pattern, usually a postorder shape.

Mirror image example: To mirror a tree, swap the left and right children of every node. mirror(t): if t == NULL return; mirror(t->left); mirror(t->right); swap(t->left, t->right). The mirror of our tree has A with left C and right B; C's left child is F; B has left E and right D. Its inorder is F C A E B D, which is exactly the reverse of the original inorder. That is a nice way to check your answer.

Real life example 1, calculating folder sizes: When Windows shows the size of your 'University' folder, it must add up the sizes of all the files inside, including those in nested folders like 'Semester 3' and 'Lab reports'. It cannot know a folder's total until it has finished all its subfolders, so it works in postorder: children first, then the parent. Deleting a folder works the same way: delete the contents first, then the empty folder.

Real life example 2, a table of contents: A textbook's table of contents is a tree: chapters, sections inside chapters, and subsections inside sections. When the publisher prints the contents page, it writes 'Chapter 3', then '3.1', then '3.1.1', then '3.1.2', then '3.2', which is a preorder traversal: each heading before the headings beneath it. When a school announces exam results class by class, from Class 1 to Class 10, and within each class section by section, that is more like a level order traversal.

Real life example 3, a calculator app: When you type (12 + 8) × (10 − 4) into a scientific calculator app, it can parse the input into an expression tree with × at the root. Computing the result is a postorder traversal: compute 12 + 8 = 20, compute 10 − 4 = 6, then 20 × 6 = 120. Printing the expression back neatly with brackets is an inorder traversal that adds brackets around each subtree.

Common mistakes: Visiting right before left. Forgetting that the base case is an empty subtree, not a leaf. Mixing up which order is which; remember that the name tells you where the node goes: PRE means node before, IN means node in the middle, POST means node after. Trying to do level order with recursion and a stack instead of a queue. When rebuilding a tree from postorder and inorder, taking the root from the front instead of the end.

What exams ask: Give the preorder, inorder, postorder and level-order traversals of a given tree. Write recursive algorithms for the three depth-first traversals and an algorithm for level order using a queue. Write a non-recursive inorder traversal using a stack. Construct a binary tree from given inorder and preorder (or postorder) sequences. Draw the expression tree for an expression and write its prefix and postfix forms. Write functions to count nodes, count leaves or find the height.

Recap: Traversals visit every node once. Preorder is node-left-right, inorder is left-node-right, postorder is left-right-node, and level order goes level by level using a queue. All run in O(n) time; recursive versions use O(h) stack space. Inorder plus preorder or postorder rebuilds a unique tree. Expression trees link preorder, inorder and postorder to prefix, infix and postfix. Next, we add an ordering rule to binary trees and get the binary search tree, where inorder gives sorted output.
key_points: Preorder: node, left, right. Inorder: left, node, right. Postorder: left, right, node.
Level order visits level by level using a queue.
All traversals take O(n) time; recursive ones use O(h) stack space.
Iterative inorder and preorder use an explicit stack instead of recursion.
Inorder plus preorder (or postorder) uniquely rebuilds a binary tree with distinct values.
Expression tree: preorder gives prefix, postorder gives postfix, inorder gives infix.
Postorder is the natural order for deleting a tree or computing sizes from children.
lessons.tip: Write the three letter patterns NLR, LNR and LRN at the top of your answer sheet before you start. The position of N tells you everything: pre, in, post.
lessons.task: Draw the tree for the expression (7 − 2) × (3 + 5). Write its preorder, inorder and postorder traversals. Then evaluate it by a postorder walk on paper and check you get 40.

quiz.q: For our example tree (A; B, C; D, E under B; F as C's right child), what is the inorder traversal?
options: A B D E C F
D B E A C F
D E B F C A
A B C D E F
quiz.explain: Left subtree (D B E), then A, then right subtree (C F).

quiz.q: Which traversal visits a binary search tree's values in sorted order?
quiz.explain: Left (smaller), node, right (larger) gives ascending order.

quiz.q: Which data structure is used for level order traversal?
quiz.explain: Nodes are processed in the order their level is reached: FIFO.

quiz.q: Which pair of traversals does NOT always determine a unique binary tree?
quiz.explain: Without inorder, a single child could be left or right.

quiz.q: In an expression tree, the postorder traversal gives the:
quiz.explain: Children before the operator is exactly postfix.

lessons.title: Binary Search Trees
lessons.content:
Play a guessing game with a friend: 'I am thinking of a number between 1 and 100.' You guess 50. 'Smaller.' You guess 25. 'Bigger.' You guess 37. Each answer throws away about half of the remaining numbers, so you will find any number in at most 7 guesses. A binary search tree is that guessing game frozen into a data structure: at every node, smaller values live on the left and bigger values live on the right, so every comparison throws part of the tree away.

What it is: A binary search tree (BST) is a binary tree where, for every node with key k, all keys in its left subtree are less than k, and all keys in its right subtree are greater than k. This must hold for whole subtrees, not just immediate children. We usually assume keys are distinct; if duplicates are allowed, a rule such as 'equal keys go right' or a count field in each node handles them.

Why it matters: A sorted array gives O(log n) search, but insertion and deletion are O(n) because of shifting. A linked list gives O(1) insertion at a known spot, but O(n) search. A BST aims to give the best of both: search, insert and delete all in O(h), where h is the height. When the tree is reasonably balanced, h is about log₂ n, so all three operations are O(log n). For a million keys, that is about 20 steps.

Building a BST by insertion: Insert 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80 in that order. 50 becomes the root. 30 < 50, so it goes left of 50. 70 > 50, right of 50. 20: less than 50, go left to 30; less than 30, so left of 30. 40: less than 50, go to 30; greater than 30, so right of 30. 60: greater than 50, go to 70; less than 70, left of 70. 80: right of 70. The result is a perfect tree of height 2 with root 50, level one 30 and 70, and leaves 20, 40, 60, 80.

Searching: To search for key x, start at the root. If the tree is empty, x is not there. If x equals the node's key, found. If x is smaller, search the left subtree; if larger, search the right subtree. search(t, x): while t != NULL and t->key != x: t = (x < t->key) ? t->left : t->right; return t. To find 60 in our tree: 60 > 50 go right to 70; 60 < 70 go left to 60; found in 3 comparisons. To find 65: 50, 70, 60, then 60's right is NULL, so not found.

Insertion: Insertion is a search that fails, followed by attaching the new node where the search fell off the tree. insert(t, x): if t == NULL return newNode(x); if x < t->key, t->left = insert(t->left, x); else if x > t->key, t->right = insert(t->right, x); return t. Inserting 65 into our tree: 50 right, 70 left, 60 right, empty, so 65 becomes the right child of 60. New nodes are always added as leaves.

Minimum and maximum: The smallest key is found by starting at the root and always going left until there is no left child: 50, 30, 20, so the minimum is 20. The largest key is found by always going right: 50, 70, 80. Both take O(h). This is a direct consequence of the BST rule: everything smaller is to the left.

Inorder gives sorted order: Because every left subtree is smaller and every right subtree is larger, an inorder traversal (left, node, right) of a BST visits the keys in increasing order. For our tree: 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80. This gives a simple sorting method, called tree sort: insert all items into a BST, then do an inorder traversal. With a balanced tree that is O(n log n).

Inorder successor: The successor of a node is the next larger key. If the node has a right subtree, the successor is the minimum of that right subtree: go right once, then all the way left. The successor of 50 is: go right to 70, then left to 60, so 60. If the node has no right subtree, the successor is the nearest ancestor for which the node lies in its left subtree. The successor of 40 is 50, because 40 is in 50's left subtree. The predecessor works the same way in mirror image.

Deletion, case 1, a leaf: Deleting a node with no children is easy: remove it and set its parent's pointer to NULL. Deleting 20 from our tree just makes 30's left pointer NULL.

Deletion, case 2, one child: If the node has exactly one child, connect its parent directly to that child, skipping the node, like removing a link from a chain. If 30 had only a right child 40, deleting 30 would make 50's left pointer point to 40. The BST rule still holds, because everything in that subtree was already less than 50.

Deletion, case 3, two children: This is the tricky case. To delete a node with two children, find its inorder successor (the smallest key in its right subtree), copy the successor's key into the node, and then delete the successor from the right subtree. The successor has no left child (it is the minimum there), so deleting it is case 1 or case 2. Example: delete 50 from our tree. Its successor is 60. Copy 60 into the root, then delete the old 60 leaf. The new root is 60 with left subtree 30 (20, 40) and right subtree 70 (80). Using the inorder predecessor (the largest key in the left subtree) instead also works.

Deletion code shape: delete(t, x): if t == NULL return NULL; if x < t->key: t->left = delete(t->left, x); else if x > t->key: t->right = delete(t->right, x); else: if t->left == NULL: return t->right (after freeing t); if t->right == NULL: return t->left (after freeing t); s = min(t->right); t->key = s->key; t->right = delete(t->right, s->key). return t. Writing it recursively and returning the new subtree root keeps the parent's pointer updated automatically.

The height problem: All BST operations cost O(h). But h depends on the insertion order. Insert 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 in increasing order: each new key goes to the right of the previous one, and the tree becomes a right-skewed chain of height 4, exactly like a linked list. Search becomes O(n). Sorted or nearly sorted input, which is very common in real life (think of roll numbers or dates), produces the worst case.

Average versus worst case: If keys arrive in random order, the expected height of a BST is O(log n), so average search, insert and delete are O(log n). But the worst case is O(n). We cannot always control the input order, so for guaranteed performance we need self-balancing trees, like the AVL tree in the next lesson, which rearrange themselves to keep h = O(log n) after every insertion and deletion.

Checking whether a tree is a BST: A common mistake is to check only that each node's left child is smaller and right child is larger. That is not enough: in a tree with root 50, left child 30, and 30's right child 60, every parent-child pair looks fine, yet 60 is in 50's left subtree, which breaks the rule. The correct check passes allowed ranges down: the root may be anything; its left subtree must be within (−∞, 50); 30's right subtree must be within (30, 50); 60 is outside, so it is not a BST. Alternatively, do an inorder traversal and check that the output is strictly increasing.

Other BST operations: Range queries, such as 'print all keys between 35 and 65', walk only the parts of the tree that can contain such keys, skipping whole subtrees. Floor and ceiling find the largest key ≤ x or the smallest key ≥ x. Counting keys less than x, or finding the k-th smallest, become efficient if each node also stores the size of its subtree. These are why ordered maps in libraries, like C++'s std::map and Java's TreeMap, are built on balanced BSTs.

Real life example 1, a dictionary app: A Bangla-English dictionary app needs to look up words, add new ones, and also show words in alphabetical order or suggest nearby words when you misspell. A BST keyed by the word does all of this: search follows comparisons, insertion adds a leaf, an inorder traversal lists words alphabetically, and the successor and predecessor of a missing word are natural 'did you mean' suggestions. A hash table would be faster for exact lookups but cannot list words in order.

Real life example 2, ranking cricketers by runs: A sports website keeps players ordered by total runs in the BPL season. When a player scores, their total changes: delete the old entry and insert the new one. The top scorer is the maximum (go right), and 'everyone between 300 and 400 runs' is a range query. Keeping the tree balanced ensures that even with thousands of players, every update takes only a handful of steps.

Real life example 3, the guessing-game toy: The '20 questions' style toys that guess the animal you are thinking of follow a decision tree of yes/no questions. When the questions split the possibilities into two similar-sized groups, around 20 questions can tell apart about a million possibilities (2^20 is about one million). That is the same power of halving that a well-balanced BST gives.

Common mistakes: Checking the BST property only between parent and child. Forgetting to update the parent's pointer after deletion. In case 3 deletion, copying the successor's key but forgetting to delete the successor node. Assuming BST operations are always O(log n); that is only true when the tree is balanced. Inserting a duplicate key without a rule, which can break searching.

What exams ask: Define a BST. Construct a BST by inserting a given sequence of keys, and show the tree after each insertion. Delete given keys, covering all three cases, and draw the result. Write algorithms for search, insertion and deletion. Find the minimum, maximum, inorder successor and predecessor. Explain the best, average and worst case complexities and why the worst case happens. Write a function to check whether a binary tree is a BST.

Practice: Insert 45, 25, 65, 15, 35, 55, 75, 30 into an empty BST. Then delete 25 (two children; successor is 30, the minimum of 25's right subtree). Answer: after deletion, 30 replaces 25, and 35's left child (the old 30) is removed, so 30 now has left child 15 and right child 35. The inorder traversal is 15, 30, 35, 45, 55, 65, 75, sorted as expected.

Recap: A BST keeps smaller keys on the left and larger keys on the right of every node, for whole subtrees. Search, insert, delete, minimum, maximum and successor all walk one path, costing O(h). Deletion has three cases: leaf, one child, and two children (replace with the inorder successor). Inorder traversal outputs the keys sorted. Random insertions give height about log n, but sorted insertions give a skewed tree with height n − 1, which motivates balanced trees, our next topic.
key_points: In a BST, all keys in the left subtree are smaller and all in the right subtree are larger, for every node.
Search, insert and delete each follow one path: O(h) time.
New keys are always inserted as leaves.
Minimum: keep going left; maximum: keep going right.
Inorder traversal of a BST gives keys in sorted order.
Delete with two children: replace with the inorder successor, then delete the successor.
Sorted input makes a skewed BST with O(n) operations; balanced trees fix this.
lessons.tip: For deletion questions, always say which case you are in (leaf, one child, two children) and name the successor you used. Examiners give step marks for the reasoning, and it stops you from forgetting the second deletion in case 3.
lessons.task: Insert the ages of 8 family members or friends into a BST on paper, in the order you think of them. Then draw a second BST with the same ages inserted in increasing order. Compare the heights of the two trees.

quiz.q: In a BST, where is the minimum key found?
quiz.explain: Keep going left; everything smaller lives to the left.

quiz.q: Inserting 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 in that order into an empty BST gives a tree of height:
quiz.explain: Each key goes right of the previous one, forming a chain of 5 nodes with 4 edges.

quiz.q: When deleting a node with two children, which node usually replaces it?
quiz.explain: The smallest key in the right subtree keeps the BST order.

quiz.q: Which traversal of a BST outputs keys in increasing order?
quiz.explain: Left (smaller), node, right (larger).

quiz.q: What is the worst-case time to search in a BST with n nodes?
quiz.explain: A skewed BST has height n − 1, so search may visit every node.

lessons.title: Balanced Trees: AVL and Red-Black
lessons.content:
Think of a bamboo pole carried by a rickshaw van. If too many sacks pile up on one side, the van tilts and becomes hard to ride. A smart van driver keeps shifting sacks from the heavy side to the light side so the load stays balanced, and the ride stays smooth no matter how much is added. A balanced binary search tree does the same thing: every time you insert or delete, it checks whether one side has become too heavy and quietly shifts nodes around to keep the tree short.

The problem we are solving: In the last lesson we saw that a BST's operations cost O(h), and that inserting keys in sorted order produces a skewed tree with height n − 1. For a million keys, that means a million steps per search instead of about 20. Real data often arrives sorted or nearly sorted: roll numbers, timestamps, invoice numbers. We need a BST that guarantees h = O(log n) whatever the insertion order.

Self-balancing trees: A self-balancing BST performs a little extra work during insertion and deletion to keep its height logarithmic. The two classic designs taught in data structures courses are the AVL tree and the red-black tree. Both still obey the BST rule, so search works exactly as before; only insert and delete gain a fix-up step. The key tool for fixing is the rotation.

AVL tree, what it is: Invented in 1962 by Adelson-Velsky and Landis (hence AVL), it was the first self-balancing BST. For every node, define the balance factor as height(left subtree) − height(right subtree), using height(empty) = −1. An AVL tree requires every node's balance factor to be −1, 0 or +1. In words: at every node, the two subtrees' heights differ by at most one.

Balance factor example: A node with a left child that is a leaf and no right child has balance factor 0 − (−1) = 1: fine. A node with a left child of height 1 and no right child has balance factor 1 − (−1) = 2: not allowed. After an insertion, only the nodes on the path from the new leaf up to the root can change height, so only they need their balance factors checked.

Why AVL height is logarithmic: Let N(h) be the minimum number of nodes in an AVL tree of height h. The sparsest such tree has a root, one subtree of height h − 1 and the other of height h − 2, each as sparse as possible: N(h) = N(h − 1) + N(h − 2) + 1, with N(0) = 1 and N(1) = 2. That gives 1, 2, 4, 7, 12, 20, 33, ..., which grows like the Fibonacci numbers, exponentially. So an AVL tree with n nodes has height at most about 1.44 log₂ n. For a million keys, that is at most about 28 levels.

Rotations: A rotation is a local rearrangement of a few pointers that changes the shape of the tree while keeping the BST order. A right rotation at node X, whose left child is Y: Y moves up to X's place, X becomes Y's right child, and Y's old right subtree becomes X's new left subtree. A left rotation is the mirror image. Each rotation changes only a constant number of pointers, so it is O(1).

Checking a rotation keeps BST order: In a right rotation at X with left child Y, call Y's subtrees A (left) and B (right), and X's right subtree C. Before: A < Y < B < X < C. After: Y is on top, A on its left, X on its right, B as X's left and C as X's right. Reading inorder: A, Y, B, X, C, the same order. The sorted order is preserved, only the heights change. That is the magic of rotations.

The four imbalance cases: After inserting into an AVL tree, walk up from the new node and find the first node with balance factor +2 or −2; call it Z. There are four cases, named by the path from Z towards the new node. LL: the new node went into the left subtree of Z's left child. RR: into the right subtree of Z's right child. LR: into the right subtree of Z's left child. RL: into the left subtree of Z's right child.

Fixing LL and RR: LL is fixed by a single right rotation at Z. Example: insert 30, 20, 10. Node 30 gets balance factor +2 with the path left-left. Rotate right at 30: 20 becomes the root, with 10 on the left and 30 on the right. RR is the mirror: insert 10, 20, 30, node 10 gets −2 with the path right-right, so rotate left at 10, and again 20 becomes the root with children 10 and 30.

Fixing LR and RL: These zig-zag cases need a double rotation. LR: first a left rotation at Z's left child, which turns it into an LL shape, then a right rotation at Z. Example: insert 30, 10, 20. Node 30 is +2, path left-right. Rotate left at 10, giving 30 with left child 20 and 20's left child 10; then rotate right at 30. Result: 20 at the root, 10 and 30 as children. RL is the mirror: insert 10, 30, 20, rotate right at 30, then left at 10, and 20 again ends up at the root.

A longer trace: Insert 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 25 into an empty AVL tree. After 10, 20, 30: RR at 10, rotate left, giving 20 (10, 30). Insert 40: it goes right of 30; balance factors are −1 at 30 and 20, which is fine. Insert 50: right of 40; now 30 has −2, an RR case, so rotate left at 30, giving 20 (10, 40 (30, 50)). Insert 25: 25 > 20, < 40, < 30, so it becomes 30's left child. Now 20 has balance factor 0 − 2 = −2, and the path is right then left: an RL case. Rotate right at 40, then left at 20. Final tree: 30 at the root, 20 (10, 25) on the left and 40 (with right child 50) on the right. Height 2 for 6 nodes.

Cost of AVL insertion: Inserting goes down one path, O(log n). Walking back up to update heights and balance factors is also O(log n). At most one single or double rotation is needed per insertion, because after it the subtree's height returns to what it was before the insertion. So insertion is O(log n) in the worst case, guaranteed.

AVL deletion: Delete as in an ordinary BST (the three cases), then walk up from the removed position, updating heights and fixing any node with balance factor ±2 using the same four rotation cases. Unlike insertion, a deletion may need rotations at several levels on the way up, but there are at most O(log n) of them, so deletion is still O(log n). Exams usually focus on insertion traces, with deletion explained in words.

Red-black trees, the idea: A red-black tree is another self-balancing BST, with slightly looser balance but fewer rotations on average. Each node is coloured red or black, with these rules: the root is black; a red node cannot have a red child; and every path from a node down to a NULL descendant contains the same number of black nodes. NULL leaves count as black. These rules guarantee that the longest path is at most twice the shortest, so the height is at most 2 log₂(n + 1).

Red-black in practice: Insertions and deletions fix violations using recolouring and at most a small constant number of rotations. Because rebalancing is cheaper, red-black trees are popular in libraries: C++'s std::map and std::set and Java's TreeMap are typically implemented as red-black trees, and the Linux kernel uses them in several places, including its process scheduler. AVL trees are more strictly balanced, so lookups can be slightly faster, which suits read-heavy workloads. Most courses teach AVL in detail and red-black at the level of rules and properties.

AVL versus red-black, a quick comparison: Both give O(log n) search, insert and delete in the worst case. AVL height is at most about 1.44 log₂ n; red-black height is at most 2 log₂(n + 1). AVL may rotate more on insert and delete; red-black usually rotates less. AVL stores a height or balance factor in each node; red-black stores one colour bit. Choose AVL for many lookups and few changes; red-black for frequent changes.

Real life example 1, a bank's account index: Sonali Bank opens new accounts every day with account numbers that increase. If these were stored in a plain BST, the tree would become a long chain and looking up an account would get slower every day. With an AVL or red-black tree, each new account triggers a few rotations at most, and finding any of millions of accounts stays at around 20 to 40 comparisons. The customer at the counter never notices, which is the point.

Real life example 2, a leaderboard in a mobile game: A Ludo King style game keeps players sorted by score. Scores change constantly as games finish. A balanced BST keyed by (score, player ID) handles each update as a delete plus an insert in O(log n), finds the top player by going right, and shows 'your rank neighbours' with predecessor and successor queries. Without balancing, a burst of players with similar scores could skew the tree and freeze the leaderboard.

Real life example 3, a calendar app: Your phone's calendar keeps events sorted by start time and must answer 'what is the next event after now?' and 'what is happening between 2 pm and 5 pm?'. Events are often added in time order, which would skew a plain BST. A balanced tree keeps successor and range queries fast however you add events, which is one reason ordered maps backed by balanced trees are everywhere.

Common mistakes: Computing balance factors with a wrong height convention, or as right minus left in one place and left minus right in another. Rotating at the wrong node; always rotate at the lowest unbalanced node on the path from the insertion. Using a single rotation for an LR or RL case, which just moves the imbalance to the other side. Forgetting to update the heights of the rotated nodes, lower node first. Losing a subtree (the B subtree) during rotation.

What exams ask: Define an AVL tree and balance factor. Explain why a balanced tree is needed. Insert a sequence of keys into an AVL tree, drawing the tree and naming the rotation (LL, RR, LR, RL) after each step. Show single and double rotations with diagrams. Prove or state the height bound. State the properties of a red-black tree. Compare AVL and red-black trees.

How to draw AVL answers: After each insertion, write the balance factor next to every node on the path to the root. Circle the first node that shows +2 or −2. Write the case name and the rotation. Redraw the tree. Then recompute the balance factors to show it is balanced again. This takes a few extra seconds per step but earns full marks and catches most errors.

Recap: Plain BSTs can degrade to O(n), so self-balancing trees keep height O(log n). An AVL tree keeps every node's balance factor in {−1, 0, +1}, restoring it after insertion with one of four fixes: LL needs a right rotation, RR a left rotation, LR a left-then-right double rotation, and RL a right-then-left double rotation. Rotations are O(1) and preserve BST order. Red-black trees use colours and looser rules, rotate less, and power many standard libraries. Next, we meet a different kind of tree with a different promise: the heap.
key_points: Self-balancing BSTs keep height O(log n), so search, insert and delete are O(log n) worst case.
AVL balance factor = height(left) − height(right) must be −1, 0 or +1 at every node.
Rotations rearrange a few pointers in O(1) and preserve the inorder (sorted) order.
LL: single right rotation; RR: single left rotation.
LR: left then right rotation; RL: right then left rotation.
AVL height is at most about 1.44 log₂ n; insertion needs at most one single or double rotation.
Red-black trees: root black, no red-red parent-child, equal black height; used in std::map and TreeMap.
lessons.tip: When doing AVL insertions, write the balance factors on your drawing after every single insert, even if nothing is wrong. Spotting the first ±2 from the bottom tells you exactly where and which rotation to do.
lessons.task: Insert the numbers 50, 40, 30, 20, 10, 5 into an AVL tree on paper. After each insertion, mark balance factors and name any rotation you perform. Compare the final height with the height of a plain BST built from the same sequence.

RR, fixed by a left rotation

All leaves must be at the same depth

lessons.title: Heaps, Priority Queues and Heap Sort
lessons.content:
Picture a school sports day. The tallest student in each class stands at the front of that class's line, and the tallest of those stands on the podium. Nobody cares about the exact order of everyone else; we only guarantee that every leader is at least as tall as the people directly behind them. If the champion leaves, we quickly find the new champion by comparing just a few leaders, not the whole school. That loose but useful arrangement is a heap.

What a heap is: A binary heap is a complete binary tree that satisfies the heap property. In a max-heap, every node's key is greater than or equal to the keys of its children, so the largest key is always at the root. In a min-heap, every node's key is less than or equal to its children's keys, so the smallest key is at the root. Notice what a heap does not promise: siblings are in no particular order, and the left subtree is not smaller than the right as in a BST.

Why it matters: In lesson 13 we said a priority queue can be implemented in many ways, and the heap is the champion: peek at the max in O(1), insert in O(log n), extract the max in O(log n). Heaps also give heap sort, an O(n log n) in-place sorting algorithm, and they power Dijkstra's shortest paths, Prim's minimum spanning tree, Huffman coding, operating system schedulers, and 'top k' queries everywhere.

Stored in an array: Because a heap is a complete binary tree, it fits perfectly into an array with no gaps, as we saw in lesson 14. With 0-based indexing, the node at index i has its left child at 2i + 1, its right child at 2i + 2 and its parent at ⌊(i − 1)/2⌋. No pointers are needed, which saves memory and makes heaps fast and cache-friendly. The array [40, 30, 15, 10, 20] represents a max-heap with 40 at the root, 30 and 15 as its children, and 10 and 20 as 30's children.

Heap height: A complete binary tree with n nodes has height ⌊log₂ n⌋. A heap of a million items has height 19. Every heap operation that walks from the root to a leaf, or from a leaf to the root, therefore takes O(log n) steps. That is the source of all the heap's speed.

Insertion (sift up): To insert a key into a max-heap, put it at the end of the array, which is the next free spot in the bottom level, keeping the tree complete. Then compare it with its parent; if it is larger, swap them. Repeat until it is not larger than its parent or it reaches the root. This is called sift up, bubble up, percolate up or up-heap. It takes at most the height in swaps, O(log n).

Insertion trace: Insert 10, 20, 15, 30, 40 into an empty max-heap. [10]. Insert 20 at index 1; parent 10 is smaller, swap: [20, 10]. Insert 15 at index 2; parent 20 is bigger, stop: [20, 10, 15]. Insert 30 at index 3; parent (index 1) is 10, swap: [20, 30, 15, 10]; new parent (index 0) is 20, swap: [30, 20, 15, 10]. Insert 40 at index 4; parent (index 1) is 20, swap: [30, 40, 15, 10, 20]; parent (index 0) is 30, swap: [40, 30, 15, 10, 20]. Final heap: [40, 30, 15, 10, 20].

Extract max (sift down): The maximum is at index 0. To remove it, take the last element of the array, move it to the root, and shrink the size by one. The tree is still complete, but the root may now be too small. Compare it with its children, swap it with the larger child if that child is bigger, and repeat until it is at least as large as both children or becomes a leaf. This is sift down, also called heapify, percolate down or down-heap. O(log n).

Extract max trace: From [40, 30, 15, 10, 20], remove 40. Move the last element, 20, to the root: [20, 30, 15, 10]. Children of index 0 are 30 and 15; the larger is 30, which is bigger than 20, so swap: [30, 20, 15, 10]. Now 20 is at index 1; its only child is index 3, holding 10, which is smaller, so stop. The new heap is [30, 20, 15, 10], and 30 is correctly at the top.

Why swap with the larger child: If you swapped the root with the smaller child in a max-heap, that smaller child would become the parent of the larger one, breaking the heap property. Swapping with the larger child guarantees the new parent is at least as large as both children. In a min-heap, everything flips: swap with the smaller child, and sift up when a key is smaller than its parent.

Other operations: Peek (getMax) just reads index 0: O(1). Increase-key in a max-heap changes a key to a larger value and sifts it up. Decrease-key sifts down. Deleting an arbitrary element at index i replaces it with the last element and then sifts up or down as needed. Searching for an arbitrary key, however, is O(n): a heap is not a search tree, so it gives no help in finding anything except the top.

Build-heap in O(n): Given an unordered array, we can turn it into a heap by inserting items one by one in O(n log n). But there is a faster method. Treat the array as a complete tree as it stands; every leaf is already a valid one-node heap. Starting from the last non-leaf node, index ⌊n/2⌋ − 1, and going backwards to index 0, call sift down on each node. Example: [4, 10, 3, 5, 1] with n = 5. Start at index 1 (10): its children 5 and 1 are smaller, nothing to do. Index 0 (4): larger child is 10, swap: [10, 4, 3, 5, 1]; now 4 at index 1 has children 5 and 1, swap with 5: [10, 5, 3, 4, 1]. Done.

Why build-heap is linear: It looks like n/2 calls times O(log n), but most nodes are near the bottom, where sift down is short. About half the nodes are leaves (no work), a quarter are one level up (at most 1 swap), an eighth are two levels up (at most 2 swaps), and so on. The total, n/4 × 1 + n/8 × 2 + n/16 × 3 + ..., adds up to less than n. So build-heap runs in O(n), a favourite exam fact.

Heap sort: Heap sort uses a max-heap to sort an array in ascending order, in place. Step 1: build a max-heap from the array, O(n). Step 2: repeat n − 1 times: swap the root (the current maximum) with the last element of the heap part, shrink the heap size by one (so the maximum is now locked in its final position at the end), and sift down the new root. Each sift down is O(log n), so the total is O(n log n).

Heap sort trace: Start from the heap [10, 5, 3, 4, 1]. Swap 10 with the last element: [1, 5, 3, 4 | 10]; sift down 1: swap with 5, then with 4: [5, 4, 3, 1 | 10]. Swap 5 with 1: [1, 4, 3 | 5, 10]; sift down: swap with 4: [4, 1, 3 | 5, 10]. Swap 4 with 3: [3, 1 | 4, 5, 10]; 3 is larger than 1, no sift needed. Swap 3 with 1: [1 | 3, 4, 5, 10]. Sorted: [1, 3, 4, 5, 10].

Heap sort properties: Its worst case is O(n log n), unlike quick sort, which can degrade to O(n²). It sorts in place with O(1) extra space, unlike merge sort, which needs O(n). But it is not stable: equal keys can change their relative order. In practice it is often a bit slower than a good quick sort because it jumps around the array, which is less cache-friendly. Some library sorts, such as introsort, switch to heap sort when quick sort's recursion goes too deep.

Top k problems: To find the 10 largest items in a stream of a million numbers, keep a min-heap of size 10. For each new number, if it is bigger than the heap's minimum, replace the minimum and sift down. At the end, the heap holds the 10 largest. Cost: O(n log k), and memory only O(k). Another classic: to keep track of the median of a growing list, use a max-heap for the smaller half and a min-heap for the larger half.

Heaps in libraries: Python's heapq module provides a min-heap on top of a list, with heappush and heappop. Java's PriorityQueue is a min-heap by default; pass a comparator to make it a max-heap. C++'s std::priority_queue is a max-heap by default. Knowing which kind is the default prevents a classic bug where your 'most urgent first' code serves the least urgent first.

Real life example 1, the operating system scheduler: When your laptop runs Chrome, a music player and a virus scan, the scheduler must keep deciding which task runs next based on priority. A priority queue built on a heap lets it pick the highest-priority ready task in O(log n) and insert newly woken tasks just as fast. Real schedulers are more complex, but the 'always take the most important next' idea is a heap at heart.

Real life example 2, finding the fastest route on Google Maps: To find the quickest route from Mirpur 10 to Motijheel, Dijkstra's algorithm keeps a min-priority queue of places ordered by the best known travel time so far. Each step extracts the closest unexplored place and updates its neighbours. With a binary heap, each extraction and update costs O(log n), so even a city road network with tens of thousands of junctions is handled in a fraction of a second.

Real life example 3, an exam topper list: The education board wants the top 100 GPA scorers out of over a million SSC candidates. Sorting everyone would cost O(n log n). Keeping a min-heap of size 100 while scanning the results costs O(n log 100), and needs memory for only 100 records. When the scan ends, the heap holds exactly the top 100.

Common mistakes: Confusing a heap with a BST and expecting sorted inorder output. Swapping with the smaller child during sift down in a max-heap. Using 1-based formulas with a 0-based array. Starting build-heap from index 0 forwards instead of from the last non-leaf backwards. Claiming build-heap is O(n log n); the tight bound is O(n). Forgetting that heap sort is not stable. Mixing up the 'heap' data structure with the 'heap' memory area used by malloc.

What exams ask: Define max-heap and min-heap; explain why a heap is stored in an array. Insert a sequence of keys into a heap, showing the array after each insertion. Delete the max (or min) and show the result. Build a heap from an array using the bottom-up method. Trace heap sort. State complexities: insert, delete, build-heap, heap sort. Explain how a heap implements a priority queue.

Recap: A heap is a complete binary tree with the heap property, stored compactly in an array. The max (or min) sits at the root, readable in O(1). Insert sifts up and extract sifts down, both O(log n). Build-heap runs bottom-up in O(n). Heap sort builds a heap and repeatedly moves the max to the end, giving an in-place O(n log n) sort that is not stable. Heaps are the standard way to build priority queues, used in schedulers, shortest paths and top-k problems.
key_points: A binary heap is a complete binary tree with the heap property: parent ≥ children (max-heap) or ≤ (min-heap).
Stored in an array: children of i at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, parent at ⌊(i − 1)/2⌋.
Peek is O(1); insert (sift up) and extract (sift down) are O(log n).
In a max-heap, sift down swaps with the larger child.
Bottom-up build-heap from the last non-leaf runs in O(n).
Heap sort: build a max-heap, then repeatedly swap the root to the end and sift down; O(n log n), in place, not stable.
Heaps implement priority queues for scheduling, Dijkstra and top-k problems.
lessons.tip: Always work heap questions on the array and the tree side by side: write the array, draw the tree beneath it, and update both after every swap. Most errors come from losing track of which index is whose parent.
lessons.task: On paper, insert 12, 7, 25, 3, 18, 30 into an empty max-heap, writing the array after each insertion. Then perform extractMax twice and write the array each time.

quiz.q: In a max-heap stored in a 0-based array, where is the parent of index 7?
What is the time complexity of building a heap bottom-up from n items?
quiz.explain: Most nodes are near the bottom where sift down is short; the sum is linear.

quiz.q: After extracting the max from the max-heap [40, 30, 15, 10, 20], what is the array?
quiz.explain: Move 20 to the root, then swap it with the larger child 30.

quiz.q: Which statement about heap sort is true?
options: It sorts in place in O(n log n) worst case
quiz.explain: Heap sort is in place, O(n log n), but not stable.

quiz.q: Why is searching for an arbitrary key in a heap O(n)?
options: Heaps are stored in linked lists
The heap property orders only parents and children, not left versus right
quiz.explain: A heap gives no left-right ordering to guide the search.

lessons.title: Multiway Trees: B-Trees, B+ Trees and Tries
lessons.content:
Think about the giant ledger books in an old government office. If every page held only one name, finding a person among a million records would mean flipping through twenty levels of 'go left or right' pages, and each page fetch from the dusty shelf takes a long time. Instead, each page of the index lists many names with directions: 'A to C, see shelf 1; D to F, see shelf 2', and so on. With a hundred entries per page, three page fetches find anyone among a million. That is the idea behind B-trees: fat nodes, short trees.

Why binary trees are not enough on disk: A balanced binary search tree with a million keys has height about 20. In RAM, 20 steps take nanoseconds. But when data lives on a disk, each node visit may need a separate disk read, and a disk read is thousands to millions of times slower than a memory access. Disks also read data in blocks, often 4 KB or more at a time. So the goal changes: make each node fill a whole block with many keys, and keep the tree as short as possible.

Multiway search trees: An m-way search tree lets each node hold up to m − 1 keys in sorted order and up to m children. If a node holds keys k1 < k2 < k3, it has four children: the first covers keys less than k1, the second keys between k1 and k2, the third between k2 and k3, and the fourth greater than k3. Searching inside a node checks its keys (often by binary search), then goes down to the right child. A binary search tree is just a 2-way search tree.

B-tree, the definition: A B-tree of order m is a balanced m-way search tree with these rules. Every node has at most m children and at most m − 1 keys. Every internal node other than the root has at least ⌈m/2⌉ children. The root, if it is not a leaf, has at least 2 children. A node with k children has exactly k − 1 keys. All leaves are at the same depth. That last rule means a B-tree is always perfectly height-balanced. (Some textbooks define B-trees by a 'minimum degree t' instead of order m; the ideas are the same, so check which convention your course uses.)

Why B-trees are short: If each node has at least ⌈m/2⌉ children, the number of nodes grows by that factor at every level, so the height is O(log base m of n). With m = 100, a B-tree of height 3 can hold on the order of a million keys or more; real databases use nodes with hundreds of keys, so even billions of records need only a handful of levels. The top levels are usually cached in memory, so a lookup may need only one or two disk reads.

Searching a B-tree: Start at the root. Within the node, find the first key greater than or equal to the target. If it equals the target, found. Otherwise go down to the child just before that key (or the last child if all keys are smaller). Repeat until found or until you fall off a leaf. The number of nodes visited is the height, O(log_m n), and inside each node binary search costs O(log m).

Inserting into a B-tree: Always insert into a leaf, in sorted position. If the leaf now has more than m − 1 keys (it overflows), split it: the median key moves up into the parent, and the keys to its left and right become two separate nodes. If the parent overflows because of this, split it too, and so on upwards. If the root splits, a new root is created with one key, and the tree grows taller by one level. B-trees grow at the root, not at the leaves, which is why all leaves always stay at the same depth.

An insertion trace, order 3: In a B-tree of order 3, each node holds at most 2 keys and has at most 3 children (this is also called a 2-3 tree). Insert 10, 20: one leaf [10, 20]. Insert 30: [10, 20, 30] overflows; the median 20 moves up as a new root, with children [10] and [30]. Insert 40: [30, 40]. Insert 50: [30, 40, 50] overflows; 40 moves up, root becomes [20, 40] with children [10], [30], [50]. Insert 60: [50, 60]. Insert 70: [50, 60, 70] overflows; 60 moves up into the root, making [20, 40, 60], which also overflows; 40 moves up into a new root. Final tree: root [40]; its children [20] and [60]; [20] has children [10] and [30]; [60] has children [50] and [70]. Every leaf is at depth 2.

Deleting from a B-tree, the idea: Deletion must keep every node at or above its minimum number of keys. If a key is removed from a leaf that still has enough keys, done. If the leaf falls below the minimum, borrow a key from a sibling that has extra, rotating it through the parent. If no sibling can spare one, merge the leaf with a sibling and pull down the separating key from the parent; the parent may then underflow and need the same treatment. Deleting from an internal node first replaces the key with its predecessor or successor from a leaf. All these steps cost O(log_m n) node visits.

B+ tree: Most databases actually use a variant called the B+ tree. In a B+ tree, all the actual records (or pointers to them) are stored only in the leaves. Internal nodes hold only keys used for routing, so they can fit even more keys per node, making the tree shorter. The leaves are also linked together in a list, left to right in key order. This makes range queries very fast: find the first key with a normal search, then walk along the leaf chain.

Range query example: A bank asks 'show all transactions between 1 March and 31 March'. In a B+ tree indexed by date, the database searches down to the leaf containing 1 March, then follows the leaf links to the right, reading records until it passes 31 March. It never goes back up the tree. This is why B+ trees are the default index in many relational databases, including MySQL's InnoDB storage engine, and are used in many file systems too.

B-tree versus B+ tree: In a B-tree, keys and their data can appear in internal nodes, so a search may stop early, above the leaves. In a B+ tree every search goes all the way to a leaf, but internal nodes are smaller, the tree is shorter, and sequential access is easy thanks to the leaf links. Exams like to ask for this comparison in a table: where data is stored, whether leaves are linked, whether keys repeat (in a B+ tree, routing keys in internal nodes also appear in leaves), and range query performance.

Tries, a tree for words: A trie (from 'retrieval', often pronounced 'try') stores strings by their characters. Each edge is labelled with a character, and a path from the root spells a prefix. A node is marked as 'end of word' if the path to it spells a whole stored word. For example, storing cat, car and cart: the root has a child 'c', which has a child 'a', which has two children 't' (end of 'cat') and 'r' (end of 'car'); 'r' has a child 't' (end of 'cart').

Trie operations: To search for a word of length L, follow L edges from the root; if any edge is missing, the word is absent; at the end, check the end-of-word mark. Insertion follows the same path, creating missing nodes, and sets the mark. Both take O(L) time, independent of how many words are stored. Listing all words with a given prefix, like 'ca', means walking to the node for the prefix and then traversing everything below it.

Trie trade-offs: Tries are fast for prefix searches and autocomplete, and they naturally list words in alphabetical order with a preorder traversal. But they can use a lot of memory: if each node has an array of 26 child pointers for English letters, most of those pointers are NULL. For Bangla, with many more characters, the waste is worse. Common fixes store children in a small hash map or sorted list, or compress chains of single-child nodes into one edge, which gives a compressed trie or radix tree.

Real life example 1, the National ID database: Bangladesh's national ID system stores records for more than a hundred million citizens. Looking up a citizen by NID number must be fast even though the data lives on disks. A B+ tree index on the NID number lets the database find any record by reading only a few blocks, and lets officials list, for example, all IDs issued within a number range by walking along the leaf chain.

Real life example 2, autocomplete in a Bangla keyboard: When you type 'বাং' on a phone keyboard, suggestions like 'বাংলা' and 'বাংলাদেশ' pop up instantly. A trie (or a compressed form of it) built from a dictionary lets the keyboard walk down three characters and then collect the most common completions below that node. Each keystroke just moves one step deeper, which is why suggestions keep up with your typing.

Real life example 3, a phone contact search: Typing '017' into the dialer to filter contacts by number prefix is another trie-like search. Typing 'Ra' in the name search works the same way. Since the time depends on the length of what you type rather than on the number of contacts, the search feels instant whether you have 50 contacts or 5,000.

Common mistakes: Confusing the order of a B-tree (maximum children) with the maximum number of keys (one less). Splitting at the wrong key; always push up the median. Forgetting that B-trees grow at the root and that all leaves stay at the same depth. Thinking B-trees are for RAM; their main motivation is disk and block storage. In tries, forgetting the end-of-word mark, so that 'car' would wrongly be found just because 'cart' was inserted.

What exams ask: Define an m-way search tree and a B-tree of order m, with its properties. Insert a sequence of keys into a B-tree of order 3, 4 or 5, drawing each split. Explain deletion with borrowing and merging. Compare B-trees and B+ trees. Explain why B-trees are used in databases and file systems. Define a trie, draw one for a set of words, and give the complexity of search and insertion.

A drawing habit for B-tree inserts: Write each node as a box with its keys separated by bars, like [20 | 40]. When a node overflows, draw it once with the extra key, circle the median, and draw the two halves below with the median moving up. Showing the overflow and the split separately earns step marks and makes errors obvious.

Recap: Multiway trees store many keys per node to stay short, which matters when every node visit is a slow disk read. A B-tree of order m keeps nodes between half full and full, keeps all leaves at the same depth, and grows by splitting at the root, giving O(log_m n) operations. B+ trees keep data only in linked leaves, making them ideal for database indexes and range queries. Tries store strings character by character, giving O(L) search and fast prefix queries such as autocomplete.
key_points: Multiway trees hold many keys per node, keeping height small for disk-based data.
B-tree of order m: at most m children and m − 1 keys per node; internal nodes at least ⌈m/2⌉ children; all leaves at one depth.
Insertion goes into a leaf; overflow splits the node and pushes the median up; the tree grows at the root.
B-tree operations take O(log_m n) node visits.
B+ trees store data only in leaves and link leaves for fast range queries; used in database indexes.
A trie stores strings by characters; search and insert take O(L) for a word of length L.
Tries power prefix search and autocomplete but can waste memory without compression.
lessons.tip: In B-tree problems, write the maximum and minimum number of keys per node for your order before you begin. With those two numbers in front of you, you will never split too early or too late.
lessons.task: Insert 5, 15, 25, 35, 45, 55, 65, 75 into a B-tree of order 3 on paper, drawing every split. Then draw a trie for the words to, tea, ten, in and inn, marking the end-of-word nodes.

quiz.q: In a B-tree of order 5, what is the maximum number of keys in a node?
quiz.explain: Order m allows at most m − 1 keys per node.

quiz.q: When a B-tree node overflows during insertion, what happens?
options: It splits and the median key moves up to the parent
The tree is rebuilt from scratch
A rotation is performed as in AVL trees
quiz.explain: Splitting and pushing up the median keeps all leaves at the same depth.

quiz.q: Why are B-trees preferred for databases stored on disk?
options: They keep the height small so fewer slow disk reads are needed
quiz.explain: Fat nodes match disk blocks and make the tree very short.

quiz.q: What is a key feature of a B+ tree?
options: Data is stored only in the root
Leaves are never at the same level
All data is in the leaves, which are linked for range scans
quiz.explain: Internal nodes route; linked leaves give fast sequential access.

quiz.q: Searching for a word of length L in a trie takes:
quiz.explain: You follow one edge per character, regardless of how many words are stored.

lessons.title: Hashing and Hash Tables
lessons.content:
Picture the cloakroom at a wedding hall. You hand over your bag and receive a token with a number, say 47. Later you give back the token, and the attendant walks straight to hook 47. Nobody searches the whole room, and nobody keeps the bags sorted. The number on the token tells exactly where your bag is. A hash table works the same way: a small calculation on the key tells us which slot to look in, so finding things takes about the same time whether there are ten items or ten million.

What it is: A hash table stores key-value pairs in an array of slots (also called buckets). A hash function takes a key, like a phone number, a name or a student ID, and turns it into an array index. To insert, compute the index and store the pair there. To search, compute the same index and look there. When things go well, insert, search and delete all take O(1) time on average, which beats the O(log n) of balanced trees.

Why it matters: Hash tables are probably the most used data structure in practical programming. Python's dict and set, Java's HashMap and HashSet, C++'s unordered_map and JavaScript objects are all hash tables underneath. They power database lookups, caches, compilers' symbol tables (mapping variable names to information), spell checkers, counting word frequencies, and detecting duplicates. Interviewers love them because many O(n²) problems become O(n) with a hash table.

The ideal and the problem: If keys were small integers, say roll numbers from 1 to 100, we could use a direct-address table: an array of size 101 where key k lives in slot k. That is perfect O(1). But real keys come from huge ranges: an 11-digit mobile number has 10^11 possible values, and we might only store a few thousand. We cannot make an array that big. So we use a smaller table of size m and a hash function that squeezes the huge key space into indices 0 to m − 1.

Hash functions, division method: The simplest is h(k) = k mod m. With m = 10, the key 1234 goes to slot 4. But m = 10 is a poor choice, because the slot then depends only on the last digit, and real data often has patterns in its last digits. A common recommendation is to choose m as a prime number not too close to a power of 2. With m = 7, the key 50 goes to 50 mod 7 = 1, and 700 goes to 0.

Other hash function methods: The multiplication method computes h(k) = ⌊m × (k × A mod 1)⌋ for a constant A between 0 and 1 (a value near 0.618 is often suggested); 'mod 1' means keeping only the fractional part. Here m can be any size. The mid-square method squares the key and takes digits from the middle: 3205² = 10272025, and the middle two digits give 72. The folding method splits the key into parts and adds them: 123456789 becomes 123 + 456 + 789 = 1368, then take it mod m. Exams often ask you to name and apply these methods.

Hashing strings: For a string key like a name, we must first turn the characters into a number. A popular approach treats the string as digits in some base: for 'cat', compute ((c × 31 + a) × 31 + t) using character codes, then take the result mod m. Simply adding the character codes is a weak hash, because 'abc' and 'cba' would collide. A good hash function should be fast to compute and should spread keys evenly over the table, so that every slot is about equally likely.

Collisions: Since many keys map into few slots, two different keys will sometimes get the same index. That is a collision. With m = 7, the keys 50 and 85 both hash to 1. Collisions are unavoidable when there are more possible keys than slots (the pigeonhole principle), and they happen surprisingly early: in a room of only 23 people, the chance that two share a birthday is already over 50 percent. So every hash table needs a collision resolution strategy. There are two main families: separate chaining and open addressing.

Separate chaining: Each slot holds a linked list (a chain) of all the pairs that hash there. Insert adds to the chain (at the front for O(1)). Search computes the slot and scans its chain. Delete removes the node from the chain. Example with m = 7 and keys 50, 700, 76, 85, 92, 73, 101: slot 0 holds 700; slot 1 holds 50, 85, 92; slot 3 holds 73, 101; slot 6 holds 76; other slots are empty. Chaining is simple, deletion is easy, and the table never 'fills up', but each node costs a pointer and chains may be scattered in memory.

Load factor: The load factor α = n / m is the average number of keys per slot. With chaining, an unsuccessful search scans a whole chain, about α nodes on average, and a successful one scans about half a chain plus one, so the expected time is O(1 + α), assuming the hash function spreads keys evenly. If we keep α below a constant, for example by growing the table, operations stay O(1) on average. In the worst case, if every key lands in the same slot, the table degrades to a single linked list and search is O(n).

Open addressing: Here all pairs live directly in the array, with no chains. When the home slot is taken, we probe other slots in a fixed sequence until we find an empty one. Searching follows the same sequence until it finds the key or hits an empty slot (which proves the key is absent). The table can never hold more than m items, so α must stay below 1, and in practice it is kept well below that, often around 0.5 to 0.75.

Linear probing: Try h(k), then h(k) + 1, h(k) + 2, and so on, wrapping around mod m. Insert 50, 700, 76, 85, 92, 73, 101 into a table of size 7. 50 to slot 1; 700 to slot 0; 76 to slot 6; 85 hashes to 1 (taken), so slot 2; 92 hashes to 1, slots 1 and 2 taken, so slot 3; 73 hashes to 3 (taken), so slot 4; 101 hashes to 3, slots 3 and 4 taken, so slot 5. Final table: 700, 50, 85, 92, 73, 101, 76. Linear probing is simple and cache-friendly, but suffers from primary clustering: occupied slots bunch together into long runs, and any key landing in a run must walk to its end, making the run even longer.

Quadratic probing: Try h(k), h(k) + 1², h(k) + 2², h(k) + 3², ... mod m. The jumps grow, so keys escape clusters faster. With m = 7, after 50 in slot 1 and 85 in slot 2 (1 + 1), the key 92 tries slot 1, then 2, then 1 + 4 = 5, landing in slot 5. Quadratic probing avoids primary clustering, but keys with the same home slot still follow the same sequence, called secondary clustering. It also may fail to find an empty slot even when some exist, unless the table size and load factor are chosen carefully (for example, a prime m and α at most one half guarantee an empty slot is found).

Double hashing: Use a second hash function to choose the step size: probe h1(k), h1(k) + h2(k), h1(k) + 2 × h2(k), ... mod m. Different keys with the same home slot now get different step sizes, which removes both kinds of clustering. h2(k) must never be 0; a common choice is h2(k) = R − (k mod R) for a prime R smaller than m. Example with m = 7 and R = 5: for 92, h1 = 1 and h2 = 5 − (92 mod 5) = 5 − 2 = 3, so the probes are 1, 4, 0 (7 mod 7), and so on.

Deleting with open addressing: You cannot simply empty a slot, because that would break probe sequences: a later search would stop at the empty slot and wrongly report that a key further along is absent. Instead, mark the slot with a special 'deleted' marker, often called a tombstone. Searches skip over tombstones; insertions may reuse them. If many tombstones pile up, the table is rebuilt.

Rehashing: When the load factor gets too high, performance drops, so the table is resized, typically to about double the size (often the next prime), and every key is reinserted using the new m, because each key's slot depends on m. Rehashing costs O(n), but as with dynamic arrays it happens rarely enough that insertion stays O(1) amortized. Java's HashMap, for example, by default resizes when its load factor passes 0.75.

Hash tables versus balanced trees: Hash tables give O(1) average lookups, but their worst case is O(n), they keep no order, and range queries like 'all keys between 100 and 200' are slow. Balanced BSTs give guaranteed O(log n) and keep keys sorted, supporting min, max, successor and range queries. Choose a hash table for pure lookups by exact key; choose a balanced tree when order matters.

Real life example 1, bKash checking a mobile number: When you send money, the system must check in an instant whether the receiver's number has an account. Keeping all registered numbers in a hash table means each check is one hash computation and a quick look in one slot, regardless of how many tens of millions of accounts exist. A sorted list would need about 25 comparisons per check, and an unsorted list could need millions.

Real life example 2, counting votes or words: Suppose a newspaper wants to know which words appear most often in a year of articles. Scan each word and use a hash table mapping word to count: if the word is present, add one; otherwise insert it with count 1. With n words in total, the whole job is O(n) on average. The same pattern counts votes per candidate, sales per product on Daraz, or visits per page on a website.

Real life example 3, a library's cache of book covers: A library app shows book cover images, which are slow to download. It keeps recently loaded covers in a hash table keyed by ISBN. Before downloading, it checks the table: if the cover is there (a cache hit), it shows it instantly. Combined with a doubly linked list for least-recently-used eviction, as we saw in lesson 8, this is the classic LRU cache.

Common mistakes: Choosing a table size like 10 or 100 with the division method, so only the last digits matter. Forgetting to wrap around with mod m during probing. Emptying a slot on deletion in open addressing instead of using a tombstone. Saying hash table search is always O(1); it is O(1) on average with a good hash function, and O(n) in the worst case. Forgetting to rehash every key when the table grows.

What exams ask: Define hashing, hash function, collision and load factor. Describe hash function methods: division, multiplication, mid-square and folding. Insert a list of keys into a table of a given size using linear probing, quadratic probing, double hashing and chaining, and draw the final table. Explain primary and secondary clustering. Explain why deletion needs special care in open addressing. Explain rehashing. Compare chaining with open addressing.

Recap: A hash table turns a key into an array index with a hash function, giving average O(1) insert, search and delete. Collisions are unavoidable and are handled by separate chaining (lists in each slot) or open addressing (linear, quadratic or double-hash probing). The load factor α = n/m controls performance; keep it low by rehashing into a bigger table. Hash tables are unbeatable for exact-key lookups but keep no order, so balanced trees remain the choice when sorted order or range queries are needed.
key_points: A hash function maps a key to an array index; average insert, search and delete are O(1).
Division method h(k) = k mod m works best with m a prime not close to a power of 2.
Collisions are unavoidable; resolve them by chaining or open addressing.
Chaining: a linked list per slot; expected time O(1 + α), where α = n/m.
Open addressing probes: linear (primary clustering), quadratic (secondary clustering), double hashing.
Open addressing deletes with tombstones; rehash into a bigger table when α gets high.
Hash tables keep no order; worst case O(n); use balanced trees for sorted or range queries.
lessons.tip: For hashing questions, draw the table as a numbered column of empty boxes first, then insert keys one at a time, writing the probe sequence next to each key (for example 92: 1 → 2 → 3). Examiners want to see the probes, not just the final table.
lessons.task: Take a table of size 11. Insert the keys 22, 1, 13, 11, 24, 33, 18, 42, 31 using h(k) = k mod 11 and linear probing, writing each probe sequence. Then redo it with chaining and compare the longest probe sequence with the longest chain.

quiz.q: With h(k) = k mod 7, which slot does the key 50 go to?
quiz.explain: 50 = 7 × 7 + 1, so the remainder is 1.

quiz.q: What is the load factor of a hash table with 30 keys and 60 slots?
Primary clustering is a problem mainly of which method?
quiz.explain: Consecutive occupied runs grow and attract more keys.
